title: Aerial Robots

mentor.name: ROTOR-4
mentor.character: Asks what the air is doing before it looks at your code, and never lets a saturated number pass as a measurement.

summary: You will build every layer that keeps a multirotor in the air: propeller thrust, the motor mixer, the rate and angle cascade, flight modes, position hold, return to home and the energy supervisor that decides when the flight is over. By the end you can fly a full mission in wind with a draining pack and tell, with numbers, the wind and the battery state at which the machine can no longer come back.

lessons.title: The Weight You Have to Beat
lessons.goal: Compute hover thrust per rotor and the thrust to weight ratio of the test frame.
lessons.theory:
A ground robot that loses power stops. An aerial robot that loses power falls. Nothing about a multirotor is stable by construction: the only thing holding 1.35 kg in the air is four propellers pushing down on the air hard enough to cancel gravity, and they have to keep doing it every millisecond of the flight.

The frame this course flies is the **Wind Gallery test frame**: a quadrotor in X layout, 1.35 kg all up, four 9x4.5 propellers on 2212 motors, a 4S 5.2 Ah pack. Its weight is `MASS * G`, about 13.24 N, and in a level hover each rotor carries a quarter of it, `MASS * G / ROTORS`.

The number that decides what the machine can do is the **thrust to weight ratio**, `MAX_THRUST_PER_MOTOR * ROTORS / (MASS * G)`. Below 1.0 it never leaves the ground. At 1.3 it is a barge that cannot correct a gust. Around 2.0 is the design point for a stable camera platform, because half the available thrust is left over for control. Racing quads sit at 6 and above, and they are unflyable by anyone who is not paying attention.

The inverse of that ratio is the **hover throttle fraction**, the stick position where the machine just floats. On this frame it lands near 0.37. That single number tells you how much control authority you have left in every direction, and it is the first thing an autopilot learns about a new airframe.

lessons.title: The Square Law
lessons.goal: Convert between rotor speed and thrust in both directions and show why the relation is not linear.
lessons.theory:
A propeller does not produce thrust in proportion to how fast it turns. It produces thrust in proportion to the **square** of how fast it turns. For a fixed pitch propeller in still air the useful model is `KF * omega * omega`, with omega in radians per second and `KF` a coefficient you measure on a thrust stand. On the 9x4.5 props of this frame `KF` is 1.1e-5 newtons per squared radian per second.

To find the hover speed you invert it: `math.sqrt(thrust / KF)`. Each rotor needs 3.31 N, so it turns at about 549 rad/s, which is 5240 rpm. That is the number you would see on a tachometer with the machine floating in front of you.

The square is not a detail, it is the reason every autopilot in this course commands **thrust**, not rotor speed. Doubling omega gives four times the thrust, so the same 100 rad/s step is worth a lot more near full throttle than near idle. A controller tuned in units of rotor speed would be four times too soft at the bottom of its range and four times too aggressive at the top.

There is a second consequence you will meet in chapter 7. Power goes roughly with the cube of omega while thrust goes with the square, so thrust gets more expensive the harder you push. A rotor at twice hover speed costs eight times the power for four times the lift.

lessons.title: Four Arms, Two Directions
lessons.goal: Lay out the X frame geometry and show that the reaction torques cancel only when all four rotors match.
lessons.theory:
The X layout puts the four rotors on the diagonals, so that a roll and a pitch each use all four motors instead of two. Rotor `i` sits at 45 plus 90 times `i` degrees around the body z axis, at a distance `ARM` from the centre, which on this frame is 0.17 m. Its x offset is therefore `ARM * math.cos(math.radians(45.0 + 90.0 * i))` and its y offset is the same with a sine. That works out at 0.120 m of leverage on each axis, not 0.17.

The spin directions are not decoration. A propeller pushing air down also drags the airframe around with it, so a rotor turning clockwise seen from above twists the body counter clockwise. If all four turned the same way the machine would spin up around z and never stop. So the two rotors on one diagonal turn one way and the two on the other diagonal turn the opposite way, which is what the `SPIN` table encodes.

The total yaw torque is then `sum(SPIN[i] * KM * w[i] * w[i] for i in range(ROTORS))`, with `KM` the drag torque coefficient of the propeller, 1.9e-7 on these blades. When all four rotor speeds are equal the four terms cancel exactly and the machine holds its heading with no yaw input at all.

That cancellation is also the yaw actuator. Speed up one diagonal, slow the other by the same amount, and the thrust stays where it was while the leftover drag torque turns the aircraft. Yaw on a multirotor is a side effect you learned to aim.

lessons.title: The Weakest Axis
lessons.goal: Compare the effective moment arm of yaw against roll and explain why yaw is given up first.
lessons.theory:
Roll and pitch are made by pushing harder on one side than the other. The lever is geometric: `ARM * math.cos(math.radians(45.0))`, which is 0.120 m on this frame. One newton of thrust difference buys 0.120 N m of roll torque.

Yaw has no lever. It is made from the propeller drag torque, and the exchange rate between thrust and yaw torque is fixed by the propeller itself: `KM / KF`, which on these blades is 0.0173 m. One newton of thrust difference buys 0.0173 N m of yaw torque, seven times less than the same newton buys in roll.

That ratio is why the mixer of chapter 1 gives yaw the lowest priority, and why a quadrotor that runs out of motor range loses its heading long before it loses its attitude. It is also why a hard yaw command visibly disturbs altitude on a cheap machine: to get any yaw torque at all the mixer has to move the rotor speeds a long way, and the thrust does not stay put while it does.

Aircraft designers cannot fix this by tuning. The only knobs are the propeller, which sets `KM / KF`, and the arm length, which sets the roll lever. A larger frame with the same props has worse yaw authority relative to roll, not better.

lessons.title: Six Places to Be, Four Ways to Push
lessons.goal: Compute the tilt and the extra thrust a horizontal acceleration costs on an underactuated airframe.
lessons.theory:
A quadrotor has six degrees of freedom in the world and four independent inputs. It cannot move sideways without first pointing somewhere else, because all four propellers push along the same body axis. There is no rotor aimed left.

So every horizontal move is a two step trade. To accelerate horizontally at `a_h` the thrust vector has to lean by `math.atan2(a_h, G)`, and the vertical component of that leaned vector still has to carry the whole weight. The total thrust required grows to `MASS * math.hypot(a_h, G)`. At half a g of lateral acceleration that is 26.6 degrees of lean and 11.8 percent more thrust than a hover.

This is the single fact that shapes the rest of the course. The position loop cannot command a force, it can only command an attitude, so it sits on top of the attitude loop instead of beside it. That is the cascade of chapter 3, and it exists because of underactuation, not because someone preferred nested loops.

It also means a tilt limit is really an acceleration limit in disguise, and a thrust limit is really a tilt limit in disguise. Chapter 3 makes you print both numbers side by side, because confusing them is how a machine ends up asking for a manoeuvre it cannot pay for.

lessons.title: Four Numbers the Whole Aircraft Obeys
lessons.goal: Turn four rotor thrusts into the collective thrust and the three body torques they produce.
lessons.theory:
Nothing above the mixer ever talks about motors. The whole flight stack commands four numbers: collective thrust along body z, and torque about x, y and z. Everything else is arithmetic on the frame geometry, and it belongs in one function that you can test on its own.

Going from the four rotor thrusts to those numbers is the **forward mix**. Collective thrust is just the sum. Roll torque is `sum(POS_Y[i] * f[i] for i in range(ROTORS))`, because a force along z applied at a positive y produces a positive torque about x. Pitch torque picks up a minus sign from the same cross product, `-sum(POS_X[i] * f[i] for i in range(ROTORS))`, and forgetting it is the classic reason a new frame pitches the wrong way on the bench.

Yaw does not come from geometry at all. It comes from propeller drag, so it uses the exchange rate of dr0-4: `sum(SPIN[i] * YAW_ARM * f[i] for i in range(ROTORS))`, with `YAW_ARM` at 0.0173 m against 0.120 m on the other two axes.

Write this direction first even though the autopilot needs the other one. It is the ground truth. Every later lesson in this chapter checks the inverse mixer by pushing its output back through these four functions and asking whether the aircraft got what was ordered.

lessons.title: The Mixer Bench
lessons.goal: Build the inverse mixer that splits a commanded wrench into four rotor thrusts.
lessons.theory:
The controller produces a wrench and the motors need thrusts, so somebody has to invert dr1-1. On a symmetric X frame you do not need a matrix inverse, because the four sign patterns are orthogonal: each axis writes its own contribution and they never interfere.

Start from the collective, `thrust / ROTORS`, the same for every rotor. Then add the roll contribution, `S_ROLL[i] * roll / (4.0 * ROLL_ARM)`, where the four in the denominator is there because all four rotors contribute to the lever, not two. Pitch adds `S_PITCH[i] * pitch / (4.0 * ROLL_ARM)` with its own sign pattern, and yaw adds `S_YAW[i] * yaw / (4.0 * YAW_ARM)`, which uses the much smaller propeller arm and therefore asks for much bigger thrust differences.

The three sign patterns are the frame written down as numbers. `S_ROLL` is 1, 1, -1, -1 because the two front rotors are both on the positive y side. `S_PITCH` is -1, 1, 1, -1. `S_YAW` is the spin table itself. Any of the three can be written wrong and the aircraft will still lift off, which is the subject of dr1-4.

Note what the mixer does not do here: it does not check whether the result is achievable. A wrench that asks for a negative rotor thrust comes back with a negative rotor thrust. Clamping it is a separate decision with its own consequences, and it gets its own lesson.

lessons.title: From Newtons to the Wire
lessons.goal: Convert rotor thrust into a normalised motor command and measure what a linear throttle assumption costs.
lessons.theory:
The mixer speaks newtons. An ESC accepts a number between 0 and 1. Between them sits the square law of dr0-2, and skipping it is one of the most common reasons a machine that flies fine in a hover falls apart in a fast descent.

The honest conversion is `math.sqrt(max(f, 0.0) / KF) / MAX_OMEGA`, and its inverse is `KF * (u * MAX_OMEGA) ** 2`. The clamp at zero is not cosmetic: the mixer can and does ask for negative thrust, and a square root of a negative number ends the flight with a traceback instead of a landing.

Now measure the mistake. The lazy conversion is to divide the thrust by the maximum thrust and call it throttle. At hover that gives 0.372, and if you feed 0.372 to the ESC the motor actually produces 1.23 N instead of 3.31 N. The machine sits on the ground at what the controller believes is hover throttle, and the integrator winds up trying to fix it.

The correct hover command is 0.610. Notice how far it is from the middle of the stick even though the frame has a healthy thrust to weight of 2.7: the square law pushes hover up near two thirds of travel on almost every multirotor, which is why hovering with the stick at half is a sign that something is heavier than the model thinks.

lessons.title: The Sign That Flies in Simulation
lessons.goal: Show that one flipped column of the mixer leaves roll working and quietly destroys pitch.
lessons.theory:
A mixer sign error is the defect that does not announce itself. The machine still lifts off, still responds to the stick in roughly the right direction, and still holds a hover on the bench. It fails in the air, once, permanently.

Here is why it hides. Flip the sign of rotor 1 in the roll column and command a pure roll. The rotor thrusts still differ across the frame, so a roll torque still appears, at half the size. But the leftover shows up on the other axes: the real frame now produces a pitch torque of equal size and opposite sign, from a command that never mentioned pitch. The roll loop is closed and corrects itself. The pitch loop is being driven by roll and nothing in the roll loop knows.

Now the part worth remembering. A simulation that computes the resulting torque from the same table the mixer used will report a perfect pure roll and zero pitch, forever, because it is asking the liar to grade its own answer. To see the bug the plant has to use the real geometry of dr1-1 while the mixer uses its own table, so write the pitch line as `true_pitch_torque(f) if real_plant else 0.0` and run both.

This is the general shape of the trap, not a detail of quadrotors. Any model that verifies a transformation with the same matrix it applied will always agree with itself.

def true_pitch_torque(f):
    return -sum(POS_X[i] * f[i] for i in range(ROTORS))


def mix_roll(signs, thrust, roll):
    return [thrust / ROTORS + signs[i] * roll / (4.0 * ROLL_ARM) for i in range(ROTORS)]


def fly(signs, real_plant):
    roll, p, pitch, q = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    for _ in range(STEPS):
        demand = IXX * KP_RATE * (KP_ANGLE * (TARGET - roll) - p)
        f = mix_roll(signs, HOVER, demand)
        tx = true_roll_torque(f) if real_plant else demand
        ty = true_pitch_torque(f) if real_plant else 0.0
        p += tx / IXX * DT
        roll += p * DT
        q += ty / IYY * DT
        pitch += q * DT
    return math.degrees(roll), math.degrees(pitch)

lessons.title: The Ceiling Nobody Told the Controller
lessons.goal: Clamp the rotor thrusts to the physical range and report what the clamp took away on every axis.
lessons.theory:
The mixer will happily ask rotor 2 for minus 1.9 N. The motor cannot pull. Every real mixer therefore ends in `min(MAX_THRUST, max(MIN_THRUST, f))`, with `MIN_THRUST` at 0.35 N because a stopped rotor takes a fifth of a second to come back and no controller can wait that long.

That clamp is not free and it is not neutral. Command a roll of 2.5 N m at hover collective and two rotors sit comfortably inside the range while the other two get pinned at the floor. The roll you actually get is 1.96 N m, not 2.5. Worse, the two pinned rotors are now producing far more thrust than the mixer intended, so the collective jumps from 13.24 N to 17.7 N and the aircraft climbs during a manoeuvre that never asked to climb.

Print both halves. A function that reports only the clamped rotor thrusts is reporting the ceiling, not the aircraft, and a ceiling is the same number no matter what you ask for. What you want on the screen is the difference between what was ordered and what the frame produced, `roll_torque(clamped) - roll_cmd` on every axis, because that difference is the only thing the layer above can act on.

Chapter 3 comes back to this with the same warning about tilt limits. A limiter that is not reported is a lie with a plausible number attached.

lessons.title: Give Up Height Before Attitude
lessons.goal: Move the collective so the attitude torque fits inside the motor range instead of clipping it.
lessons.theory:
The clamp of dr1-5 is the worst possible way to handle a wrench that does not fit, because it damages the axis that keeps the aircraft alive. Attitude is not negotiable. Height is.

The fix is to notice that the collective is a free offset. The roll and pitch shares are differences between rotors, so sliding all four rotors up or down together does not change any torque. Compute the differential part first, then choose the per rotor collective inside the window that keeps every rotor legal: at least `MIN_THRUST - min(d)` and at most `MAX_THRUST - max(d)`. Written directly that is `min(MAX_THRUST - max(d), max(MIN_THRUST - min(d), thrust / ROTORS))`.

Ask for a 30 N climb with 1.6 N m of roll and the window closes at 5.58 N per rotor, so the collective drops from 30 N to 22.3 N. The roll comes out exactly as ordered, and the aircraft accelerates upward 5.7 m/s per second less than the pilot wanted. That is the right trade every time.

There is a limit to the trick. When the differential alone spans more than the motor range, no offset works and the window is empty, `MAX_THRUST - max(d) < MIN_THRUST - min(d)`. On this frame that happens above about 2.06 N m of roll. Past that the torque itself has to shrink, which is dr1-7.

lessons.title: Yaw Goes First
lessons.goal: Scale the yaw demand down until roll and pitch fit, and report the scale factor instead of hiding it.
lessons.theory:
When the collective offset of dr1-6 is not enough, something has to be reduced. The order is not arbitrary. Losing roll or pitch means losing the aircraft in under a second. Losing heading means the machine points the wrong way while it stays perfectly in the air. Yaw goes first, always.

Yaw is also the cheapest thing to give up because it is the most expensive thing to buy. From dr0-4, the same torque costs seven times the thrust difference on yaw as it does on roll, so a modest yaw command eats most of the motor range on its own. Ask for 1.6 N m of roll and 0.3 N m of yaw together on this frame and the two demands need 7.7 N of spread per rotor against a usable spread of 4.28 N.

The half range each axis may use is `0.5 * (MAX_THRUST - MIN_THRUST)`. Give roll and pitch what they need, then let yaw have whatever is left, so the yaw scale is `max(0.0, half - roll_part) / yaw_part`. In this case yaw comes back at 0.066 N m out of 0.3, a factor of 0.22, and roll is untouched.

Return the factor. A supervisor that sees yaw scaled to a fifth for several seconds knows the aircraft is fighting something and can say so, while a mixer that quietly clips yaw produces a machine that slowly rotates for no visible reason and a pilot who blames the compass.

lessons.title: Authority Depends on the Throttle
lessons.goal: Compute the roll torque available as a function of collective and find the throttle where control is strongest.
lessons.theory:
Control authority is not a property of the airframe. It is a property of the airframe **at the current throttle**, and it goes to zero at both ends of the stick.

At a given per rotor collective `c`, the largest symmetric spread the motors allow is `min(MAX_THRUST - c, c - MIN_THRUST)`, so the roll torque available is `4.0 * ROLL_ARM * min(MAX_THRUST - c, c - MIN_THRUST)`. At hover, `c` is 3.31 N, the floor is the binding side and you have 1.42 N m. At full throttle the ceiling is at zero distance and you have nothing at all: a quadrotor at 100 percent collective cannot roll, cannot pitch and cannot yaw. It is a rocket with a heading.

The peak sits where the two distances are equal, at a total thrust of `0.5 * (MAX_THRUST + MIN_THRUST) * ROTORS`, which is 18.5 N on this frame, around 1.4 times the weight. That is one of the real reasons the design rule for a stable machine is a thrust to weight near 2: it puts hover close to the throttle where the aircraft is most controllable, not merely airborne.

Print the whole curve, not a single number. A controller that assumes constant authority is tuned for exactly one throttle setting and is either sluggish or oscillating everywhere else, and the first place a pilot meets that is a full power climb, right where authority has collapsed.

lessons.title: The Round Trip That Must Close
lessons.goal: Push a commanded wrench through the mixer and back through the frame, and prove the loop closes only while nothing saturates.
lessons.theory:
Everything in this chapter is one claim: the mixer and the frame are inverses of each other. That claim is testable in four lines, and testing it is how you find a wrong sign, a wrong arm and a wrong yaw coefficient without leaving the desk.

Send a wrench through the mixer, clamp the result the way the hardware will, then push it back through the forward mix of dr1-1 and compare. The residual is `max(abs(a - b) for a, b in zip(back, want))`. For any command inside the envelope it comes back at the order of 1e-15, which is floating point noise and nothing else. If it comes back at 0.24 you have a sign or an arm wrong, and it will fly anyway, which is the whole problem.

Then run it again with a command outside the envelope and watch the residual explode. That is the honest result and it is the reason the test takes two cases. A round trip test that only ever runs achievable commands proves the mixer is consistent and says nothing about what the aircraft does when the pilot asks for more than it has, which is most of an interesting flight.

From here on, every layer of the stack ends at this interface: four numbers, checked against the frame, with a flag saying whether the frame could actually deliver them.

lessons.title: The Gyro Is Not Telling You Angles
lessons.goal: Convert body angular rates into Euler angle rates and find the attitude where the conversion blows up.
lessons.theory:
An MPU6000 gyro measures `p`, `q` and `r`, the rotation rates about the **body** axes, bolted to the frame and tilting with it. The attitude you want to hold is expressed in Euler angles relative to the world. These are not the same quantities and integrating one to get the other is wrong the moment the aircraft leaves level flight.

The bridge is the Euler rate transformation. Roll rate is `p + q * math.sin(phi) * math.tan(theta) + r * math.cos(phi) * math.tan(theta)`, pitch rate is `q * math.cos(phi) - r * math.sin(phi)`, and yaw rate is `(q * math.sin(phi) + r * math.cos(phi)) / math.cos(theta)`. At level attitude every correction term dies and roll rate equals `p`, which is exactly why the mistake survives a bench test and shows up in a banked turn.

Look at the tangents and the division. At 90 degrees of pitch the tangent is infinite and the cosine is zero, so the whole transformation ceases to exist. That is **gimbal lock**, and it is a property of the coordinates, not of the aircraft. The machine is perfectly happy pointing straight up. Its description is not.

A camera drone that never exceeds 35 degrees can live with Euler angles. Anything that loops, flips or recovers from an upset cannot, which is why the next lesson throws them away and uses a quaternion instead.

lessons.goal: Build the quaternion attitude error and force it to take the shorter of the two possible rotations.
lessons.theory:
A quaternion has no singularity and no ordering convention to get wrong, which is why every flight controller written after about 2010 keeps attitude as `(w, x, y, z)`. The attitude error between where you are and where you want to be is a rotation, and rotations compose by multiplication: `quat_mul(q_des, quat_conj(q_cur))`.

That product has a trap in it. Every rotation has two quaternion representations, `q` and `-q`, describing the same orientation by going round the short way or the long way. The algebra does not care. The aircraft does. Ask a machine pointing at 10 degrees to hold 350 degrees and the raw error can come back as a 340 degree turn to the left instead of a 20 degree turn to the right.

The fix is one line and it is not optional: `tuple(-v for v in e) if e[0] < 0.0 else e`. A negative scalar part means the rotation is longer than half a turn, and negating the whole quaternion gives the same orientation described the short way. Skip it and the machine will occasionally spin almost all the way around to reach a heading it was nearly at.

The size of that error in degrees is `2.0 * math.degrees(math.acos(min(1.0, abs(e[0]))))`. The clamp inside the arc cosine is there because a quaternion that has been integrated for a while is only unit length to about fifteen decimals, and the sixteenth one ends the flight with a math domain error.
lessons.task: Implement `attitude_error` with the short way fix and `error_deg`, then print the error size for a 20 degree heading change written both ways round.
lessons.hint: The sign of the scalar part is the whole test. If it is negative the quaternion is describing the long way round, and the same orientation negated describes the short one.

lessons.title: The Error the Controller Can Use
lessons.goal: Turn an error quaternion into a rotation vector and show where the small angle shortcut stops working.
lessons.theory:
A rate controller needs a vector in radians, not a quaternion. The exact conversion is the axis angle form: the angle is `2.0 * math.atan2(norm, e[0])` with `norm` the length of the vector part, and the direction is that vector part normalised. Multiply the two and you have the rotation vector, the amount of turning required about each body axis.

Almost every flight controller instead uses the shortcut `tuple(2.0 * c for c in e[1:])`, twice the vector part with no trigonometry at all. For small errors it is excellent: at 5 degrees the two agree to better than a tenth of a percent, and it costs three multiplications inside a loop that runs a thousand times a second.

The shortcut has a wall. Twice the vector part is `2 * sin(angle / 2)`, which peaks at 2.0 when the error reaches 180 degrees and then **decreases**. Ask that controller to correct a 175 degree error and it commands less than it would for a 115 degree one. The correcting torque falls off exactly where the aircraft is most upset, and an upside down machine using the shortcut recovers slowly or not at all.

So the rule is: shortcut inside the normal envelope, exact conversion anywhere an upset is possible. Chapter 8 has a machine that ends up inverted after a motor failure, and it uses the exact form.
lessons.task: Implement `rotation_vector` and `small_angle`, then print the magnitude of each for errors of 5, 90 and 175 degrees about the body x axis.
lessons.hint: The exact version needs the length of the vector part twice, once to get the angle out of the arc tangent and once to normalise the direction. Guard it, because a zero error has no axis.

value: tuple(2.0 * c for c in e[1:])

lessons.title: The Innermost Loop
lessons.goal: Close the body rate loop on the roll axis and measure the time constant it actually produces.
lessons.theory:
The rate loop is the fastest thing on the aircraft and the only loop that touches the mixer. It takes a body rate setpoint, subtracts the gyro, and produces a torque. On a rigid body with a known inertia the honest form of that command is `IXX * KP_RATE * (rate_sp - rate)`, because multiplying by the inertia turns a gain in units of one over seconds into newton metres, and makes the same gain mean the same thing on a 1.35 kg quad and on a 4 kg one.

Do the algebra of that loop and it is a first order system. The rate error decays exponentially with a time constant of `1.0 / KP_RATE` seconds, nothing else. A gain of 25 gives 40 ms, which means the machine reaches 63 percent of a commanded rate step in 40 ms and is essentially there in 120.

That is the whole design rule for this layer, and it is worth measuring rather than trusting. Run the loop, find the first sample where the rate has crossed 63.2 percent of the setpoint, and compare the time against the prediction. On the ideal model they agree to within one sample period. When they stop agreeing, something you did not model is in the loop, and dr2-5 is about the usual culprit.

Note what is missing: there is no integrator here. A rate loop with a P term and a rigid body has zero steady state error already, because the aircraft has no spring pulling it back. The I term in a real rate loop exists to fight a bent motor mount or a bad propeller, not to fix this.

lessons.title: The Motor Is Not a Wire
lessons.goal: Add the propeller spin up lag to the rate loop and measure the overshoot it introduces.
lessons.theory:
The loop of dr2-4 assumes the torque appears the instant you ask for it. It does not. An ESC changes the current quickly, but the propeller and rotor have inertia and take time to reach a new speed. On the 2212 motors and 9 inch props of this frame the thrust follows the command as a first order lag with a time constant near 30 ms, so the delivered torque is `f + (f_cmd - f) * (DT / TAU_MOTOR)` on every step, not `f_cmd`.

Thirty milliseconds sounds harmless next to a 40 ms loop time constant. It is not, because it changes the order of the system. A first order plant with proportional feedback can never overshoot. A first order plant behind a first order actuator is second order and does overshoot, and the damping ratio falls as the gain rises. At a rate gain of 40 this frame overshoots its commanded rate by about a fifth.

Measure it as `max(0.0, peak / rate_sp - 1.0)`, the fractional excess of the highest rate reached over the one commanded. Run the same gain with and without the lag and print both. The pair of numbers is the point: the ideal model says zero and always will, no matter how high you push the gain, which is exactly why tuning against an ideal model produces a machine that oscillates on the first flight.

This is the physical reason propeller size shows up in tuning guides. A larger, heavier propeller has a longer time constant, and the same gains that fly a 5 inch racer will shake a 15 inch machine to pieces.

lessons.title: The Gain the Propeller Allows
lessons.goal: Sweep the rate gain against the motor lag and pick the highest one that still meets an overshoot budget.
lessons.theory:
Tuning is not taste once you have dr2-5. The propeller time constant sets a ceiling on the rate gain, the ceiling is computable, and the computation is a sweep.

Fix the budget first. Ten percent overshoot on a rate step is a reasonable number for a camera platform: enough response to feel solid, not enough to bounce. Then run the loop of dr2-5 at a series of gains and keep the ones where `overshoot_at(k) <= MAX_OVERSHOOT`. The answer is `max(candidates)`, the fastest loop the airframe will accept.

On this frame with a 30 ms motor the answer comes out at 20, which is a rate time constant of 50 ms. Push to 25 and the overshoot passes 10 percent, push to 40 and you are at 20 percent and the machine will sound rough in the air. Nothing about that limit is a preference, and no amount of derivative term moves it much, because the lag is in the actuator and not in the measurement.

Print the whole sweep, not just the winner. The shape of the column is the useful part: it tells you how much margin the chosen gain has, and it tells you immediately what a bigger propeller will cost, because doubling the motor time constant halves the acceptable gain.

import math

IXX = 0.011
DT = 0.001
STEPS = 800
TAU_MOTOR = 0.030
RATE_SP = 3.0
GAINS = (5.0, 10.0, 15.0, 20.0, 25.0, 30.0, 40.0)

    rate, torque, peak = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    for _ in range(STEPS):

        torque = torque + (cmd - torque) * (DT / TAU_MOTOR)

print("best_gain", best_gain())

lessons.title: Tilt First, Heading Later
lessons.goal: Split the attitude error into tilt and heading and weight the heading down so the aircraft never trades one for the other.
lessons.theory:
An attitude controller handed a large error will ask for torque on all three axes at once, and the mixer of dr1-7 will then quietly scale yaw down to fit. That works, but the decision was made in the wrong place: the mixer knows about motors, not about which axis keeps the aircraft alive.

Do it properly one layer up. Split the rotation vector of dr2-3 into the part that moves the thrust direction and the part that spins about it. The tilt part is the first two components, of size `math.hypot(e_roll, e_pitch)`, and it is the only part that changes where the aircraft is going. The heading part is the third component, and a wrong heading costs nothing but a wrong picture.

So the controller emits the tilt error untouched and the heading error multiplied down, `YAW_WEIGHT * e_yaw`, with a weight around 0.4 on a camera machine. The aircraft rights itself first and turns to face the right way afterwards, using whatever authority is left. Set the weight to 1.0 and a large simultaneous error produces a torque demand that saturates the motors and gets both axes served badly.

You can see it in the numbers. With 20 degrees of error on each tilt axis and 30 degrees of heading error, the full demand asks for 4.32 rad/s against a 4.0 budget and does not fit, while the prioritised demand asks for 3.22 and does. Print both totals rather than just the flag, because the size of the gap is what tells you whether the weight is right.

lessons.title: Pointing Where You Want to Go
lessons.goal: Turn a desired acceleration vector into the roll, pitch and collective thrust that produce it.
lessons.theory:
This is the hinge of the whole aircraft. Everything above it thinks in accelerations, everything below it thinks in attitude, and the conversion happens here in three lines.

Take the acceleration you want, add gravity to it, and you have the direction the thrust vector must point. Normalise it and call it `b3`, the desired body z axis in world coordinates. Now choose the heading `psi` you want independently, because tilt and heading are separate choices, and read the Euler angles off: roll is `math.asin(b3[0] * math.sin(psi) - b3[1] * math.cos(psi))` and pitch is `math.atan2(b3[0] * math.cos(psi) + b3[1] * math.sin(psi), b3[2])`.

Run it with 2 m/s squared of desired acceleration along world x. Facing north, the machine pitches 11.5 degrees nose down and does not roll. Facing east, with the same world acceleration, it rolls 11.5 degrees and does not pitch. The world demand is identical and the attitude command is completely different, which is what those sines and cosines of `psi` are doing.

The collective comes out of the same vector: `MASS * math.sqrt(ax * ax + ay * ay + (az + G) ** 2)`, the length of the acceleration you asked for including gravity. It is not `MASS * G` and it is not `MASS * G / math.cos(tilt)` unless the vertical acceleration happens to be zero, which chapter 5 leans on when the machine is climbing.

lessons.title: The Attitude Module
lessons.goal: Assemble the whole attitude layer: desired acceleration in, body rate setpoint out, with the tilt limit reported.
lessons.theory:
Time to make the chapter into one component with a clean interface. In go a desired acceleration, a desired heading and the current attitude. Out come three body rate setpoints and a flag saying whether the tilt the aircraft asked for was legal.

The order matters. Convert the acceleration to a thrust direction, apply the tilt limit **before** deriving the attitude, build the error, prioritise the heading with dr2-7, multiply by the attitude gain, and clamp to the rate budget. Limiting after the fact would produce an attitude command the aircraft cannot hold and an error that never closes.

The limit is applied by pulling the thrust direction back toward vertical: at a tilt beyond `MAX_TILT`, rescale the horizontal part so its ratio to the vertical part is `math.tan(MAX_TILT)`. And report it. A module that clips silently is the defect of dr1-5 in a new place: the number that comes out is the ceiling, not the demand, and the layer above needs to know the difference to stop asking.

Run it with a modest demand and with one that asks for 12 m/s squared sideways. The first passes through untouched. The second comes back limited, with `tilt_limited` true, and the position loop of chapter 5 uses that flag to stop its integrator instead of winding it up against a wall it cannot move.

import math

G = 9.81
MAX_TILT = math.radians(35.0)
KP_ATT = 6.0
YAW_WEIGHT = 0.4
MAX_RATE = 4.0


def thrust_direction(ax, ay, az):
    n = math.sqrt(ax * ax + ay * ay + (az + G) ** 2)
    return (ax / n, ay / n, (az + G) / n)


def limit_tilt(b3):
    horizontal = math.hypot(b3[0], b3[1])
    tilt = math.atan2(horizontal, b3[2])
    if tilt <= MAX_TILT:
        return b3, tilt, False
    scale = b3[2] * math.tan(MAX_TILT) / horizontal
    return (b3[0] * scale, b3[1] * scale, b3[2]), MAX_TILT, True


def rate_setpoint(e_roll, e_pitch, e_yaw):
    out = (KP_ATT * e_roll, KP_ATT * e_pitch, KP_ATT * YAW_WEIGHT * e_yaw)
    return tuple(min(MAX_RATE, max(-MAX_RATE, v)) for v in out)


for name, ax in (("modest", 2.0), ("beyond_limit", 12.0)):
    b3, tilt, limited = limit_tilt(thrust_direction(ax, 0.0, 0.0))
    rates = rate_setpoint(0.0, math.atan2(b3[0], b3[2]), math.radians(30.0))
    print(name, "tilt_deg", round(math.degrees(tilt), 2), "tilt_limited", limited)
    print(name, "rates_rad_s", [round(v, 4) for v in rates])

lessons.title: Three Clocks
lessons.goal: Compute the loop rates of the cascade and how far the aircraft moves between two decisions of the outer loop.
lessons.theory:
A multirotor runs three loops at three speeds and they are not negotiable, because each one is fighting a different physical time constant. The rate loop runs at 1000 Hz because the airframe time constant is tens of milliseconds. The attitude loop runs at 250 Hz. The position loop runs at 50 Hz because the aircraft is a mass and a mass changes velocity slowly.

The design rule is separation. Each loop wants to be at least four or five times faster than the one above it, computed as `fast_hz / slow_hz`, so that from the outer loop's point of view the inner one has already finished. When the ratio drops toward two, the outer loop starts seeing the inner loop's transient as if it were the plant, and the cascade oscillates. That is dr3-8.

Separation costs something, and it is worth putting a number on it. At the 4 rad/s rate limit of dr2-9 the attitude can move `math.degrees(rate / hz)` between two position updates, which is 4.6 degrees. At 10 m/s the machine travels `speed / hz`, 0.2 m, in the same interval. The position loop is always steering an aircraft that has already moved since it last looked.

That is why the outer loop never commands anything sharp. It sets a smooth acceleration target and lets the fast loops chase it, and every limit in this chapter exists to keep what it asks for inside what the layers below can deliver in one of their own cycles.

lessons.title: The Corner of the Angle Loop
lessons.goal: Build the saturated angle loop and find the error above which it stops being proportional.
lessons.theory:
The angle loop is the simplest thing in the aircraft: an attitude error goes in, a body rate setpoint comes out, `min(MAX_RATE, max(-MAX_RATE, KP_ANGLE * error))`. There is no integrator and no derivative, because the loop below it already provides the damping and the aircraft has nothing pulling it off level.

The saturation is what makes it interesting. Below a certain error the loop is a plain proportional controller with a time constant of one over the gain. Above it the output is pinned at the rate limit and the aircraft simply slews at a constant 4 rad/s. The error where the two regimes meet is `MAX_RATE / KP_ANGLE`, 0.67 rad or 38 degrees on this tuning, and it is the single most useful number for predicting how the machine will behave in an upset.

Now measure the consequence, because the intuition is wrong. Correcting 60 degrees does not take twelve times as long as correcting 5 degrees. Most of the 60 degree correction is spent in the exponential tail below the corner, and only the first tenth of a second is rate limited, so the real ratio is closer to 2.6.

lessons.title: A Tilt Limit Is a Braking Distance
lessons.goal: Convert the tilt limit into a horizontal acceleration and into the distance the aircraft needs to stop.
lessons.theory:
Setting the maximum tilt to 35 degrees feels like a comfort setting. It is not. From dr0-5, the horizontal acceleration available is `G * math.tan(max_tilt)`, so 35 degrees is 6.87 m/s squared and that is the hardest the machine can push in any horizontal direction, forever, in both directions, including toward a wall.

Which makes the tilt limit a braking distance: `speed * speed / (2.0 * max_accel)`. At 10 m/s the aircraft needs 7.3 m to stop. At 5 m/s it needs 1.8 m, because the distance goes with the square of speed and halving the speed quarters it. Raise the limit to 45 degrees and 10 m/s becomes 5.1 m, at the cost of 41 percent more thrust to hold altitude while leaning.

Every geofence, every obstacle stop and every return to home leg in chapters 6 and 8 has this number underneath it. A fence that starts braking 5 m out with a 35 degree limit is a fence the aircraft crosses at any speed above 8.3 m/s, whatever the fence code believes.

Print the pair for both limits and both speeds. It is a four line table and it is the argument you use when somebody asks for a faster cruise on the same airframe: the cruise is free, the stopping distance is not.

lessons.title: Position, Velocity, Acceleration
lessons.goal: Build the outer chain and print the raw demand and the limited demand at every stage.
lessons.theory:
Above the attitude module of dr2-9 sit two more proportional stages. Position error becomes a velocity setpoint, `min(MAX_SPEED, max(-MAX_SPEED, KP_POS * error))`. Velocity error becomes an acceleration setpoint, `min(MAX_ACCEL, max(-MAX_ACCEL, KP_VEL * (v_sp - v)))`. The acceleration becomes a tilt, which is dr2-8, and the tilt becomes rotor thrusts, which is chapter 1.

Every stage is a proportional gain and a clamp, and the clamps are what make the chain safe. A 20 m position error at a gain of 1.0 asks for 20 m/s from an airframe rated at 8, and the velocity stage refuses. The velocity error then asks for 16 m/s squared from an airframe that has 6.87, and the acceleration stage refuses. Both refusals are correct and both of them destroy information the layer above needed.

So return both numbers at every stage. `raw` is what the controller wanted, `limited` is what it got, and the difference is the aircraft telling you it is at its limit. A cascade that returns only the limited value looks perfectly healthy at 20 m of error and at 200 m of error, because the number it prints is the clamp in both cases.

Run it at 20 m, at 5 m and at 1 m. The 1 m case passes through untouched at every stage, and that is the only regime where the gains you tuned actually describe the behaviour of the machine.

lessons.title: What the Limiter Took
lessons.goal: Fly a long dash and report how long each limiter was active and how much demand it removed.
lessons.theory:
This lesson exists because of a specific way of being wrong. A cascade prints its acceleration command during a hard manoeuvre and the number is 6.87. It prints the same number the next flight, and the next, in wind and in calm, at 40 m and at 4 m. The number is not measuring the aircraft. It is the clamp, and the clamp is a constant.

The cure is to instrument the limiter itself. Count the steps where the demand was outside the range, `abs(raw_v) > MAX_SPEED` on the velocity stage and the same on the acceleration stage, and accumulate what was thrown away with `removed += abs(raw_a) - abs(a)`. Then print the fraction of the flight each limiter was active.

On a 40 m dash this frame spends 39 percent of the run speed limited and 6 percent of it acceleration limited, in one burst at the start. That profile is the flight. If the speed limiter is active 5 percent of the time the aircraft is loafing and you could raise the cruise. If it is active 95 percent of the time the gains do nothing at all and tuning them is theatre.

The same instrument is what makes the wind estimate of chapter 6 and the failsafe of chapter 8 possible, because a limiter that has been pinned for ten seconds is not a tuning question any more, it is an aircraft that cannot do what is being asked of it.

lessons.title: The Height You Lose in a Bank
lessons.goal: Compensate the collective for tilt and measure the altitude a bank costs when you do not.
lessons.theory:
When the aircraft leans, the thrust leans with it. The vertical component is what carries the weight, and it is the total times the cosine of the tilt, so a bank that is not paid for is a descent.

The compensation is `MASS * (G + a_z) / math.cos(tilt)`, one cosine in a denominator. At 35 degrees it asks for 22 percent more thrust than a hover. At 45 degrees, 41 percent. At 60 degrees, double, which is why a 2 to 1 thrust to weight machine cannot hold altitude in a 60 degree bank at all: the compensation alone consumes everything it has, and there is nothing left for the attitude loop.

Skip the cosine and the vertical acceleration is `thrust * math.cos(tilt) / MASS - G`, which at 35 degrees is minus 1.77 m/s squared. Two seconds of banked turn and the machine is 3.5 m lower than it started, with an altitude loop chasing an error it could have predicted exactly.

That is the difference between compensating and correcting. The compensation is feed forward from a number the controller already knows, the tilt it just commanded, and it costs one division. Waiting for the altitude error to appear and fixing it afterwards costs 3.5 m and puts a bump in every turn.

lessons.title: The Setpoint That Is Already Old
lessons.goal: Feed the rate loop from a slow attitude loop and measure the step it sees, with and without interpolation.
lessons.theory:
The attitude loop produces a new rate setpoint every 4 ms. The rate loop consumes one every 1 ms. Something has to happen on the three cycles in between, and the usual answer is nothing: the old value is held. That is a **zero order hold**, and it turns a smooth command into a staircase.

The staircase is not free. The rate loop sees a step at every attitude update and responds to it with the full gain, so the motors get a burst of torque four times more often than the aircraft needs one. On a machine with a high rate gain that shows up as a fine buzz in the props and heat in the ESCs, and on a log it shows up as a rate command with a square edge every 4 ms.

The alternative costs two lines: interpolate, `prev + (nxt - prev) * frac`, and hand the rate loop a ramp instead of a step. The number that tells you it worked is the largest jump between consecutive commands, `max(abs(cmd[i] - cmd[i - 1]) for i in range(1, len(cmd)))`. Held, it equals the full attitude step. Interpolated, it is a quarter of it, exactly the separation ratio of dr3-1.

The same trick is why the position loop at 50 Hz does not shake the aircraft even though it updates once per 20 rate cycles. Somewhere between the two, someone interpolated.

lessons.title: When the Loops Stop Being Separate
lessons.goal: Run the position loop over a fast attitude loop and over a slow one, and measure the overshoot each produces.
lessons.theory:
The cascade works because the inner loop is finished before the outer loop looks again. Break that and the outer loop is no longer controlling a mass, it is controlling a mass behind a lag, and a proportional controller on a lagged plant rings.

Model the attitude layer as a first order lag on the achieved acceleration, `a + (a_cmd - a) * (DT / tau_att)`. At the tuning of dr2-6 that time constant is about 50 ms, which against a position loop with a 1 s time constant is a separation of twenty and the aircraft arrives cleanly. Slow the attitude layer to 500 ms, ten times worse, and the same position gains produce a machine that sails past the target and comes back.

Measure it as `peak / TARGET - 1.0`, the fractional overshoot of the furthest point reached. Run it for twenty seconds, not two: a lagged cascade takes several cycles to show what it is going to do, and a short window makes an oscillating system look merely slow. That mistake has been made in this course material before and it cost a wrong conclusion about a perfectly good gain.

The lesson generalises past drones. Whenever you speed up an outer loop and the machine gets worse instead of better, the separation is gone and the fix is in the inner loop, not the one you were tuning.

lessons.title: The Cascade, End to End
lessons.goal: Wire position, velocity, attitude, rate and mixer into one step function and fly it to a target.
lessons.theory:
Everything from dr0-1 to here is now one function. Position error goes in the top, four rotor thrusts come out the bottom, and each stage hands the next one a quantity the next one understands.

The chain, in the only order that works: position error to velocity setpoint, velocity error to acceleration setpoint, acceleration to tilt with the limit of dr2-9, tilt to a rate setpoint through the angle gain, rate error to torque through `IXX * KP_RATE * (rate_sp - rate)`, torque and collective to rotor thrusts through the mixer, and every rotor clamped last. The collective carries the cosine compensation of dr3-6, so it is `MASS * G / math.cos(tilt)` and not the weight.

Fly it 10 m and watch three things. The rotors stay inside their range the whole way, which means no stage asked for more than the frame has. The final position error goes under 5 cm. And the peak tilt stays at the limit rather than beyond it, because the limit was applied before the attitude command was formed and not after.

This is the aircraft as far as chapter 3 can build it. What it cannot do yet is hold that position when something pushes it, know how much battery the trip cost, or decide to go home. Those are chapters 5, 7 and 8, and they all plug into this same step function.

    v_sp = min(MAX_SPEED, max(-MAX_SPEED, KP_POS * (TARGET - x)))
    a_sp = min(MAX_ACCEL, max(-MAX_ACCEL, KP_VEL * (v_sp - v)))
    tilt = min(MAX_TILT, max(-MAX_TILT, math.atan2(a_sp, G)))
    rate_sp = min(MAX_RATE, max(-MAX_RATE, KP_ANGLE * (tilt - pitch)))
    torque = IXX * KP_RATE * (rate_sp - q)
    collective = MASS * G / math.cos(tilt)
    f = [collective / ROTORS + S_PITCH[i] * torque / (4.0 * ROLL_ARM) for i in range(ROTORS)]
    f = [min(MAX_THRUST, max(MIN_THRUST, v)) for v in f]
    return f, torque, collective, tilt


x, v, pitch, q = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
peak_tilt, peak_f, inside = 0.0, 0.0, True
for _ in range(STEPS):
    f, torque, collective, tilt = step(x, v, pitch, q)
    inside = inside and max(f) < MAX_THRUST and min(f) > MIN_THRUST
    peak_tilt = max(peak_tilt, abs(tilt))
    peak_f = max(peak_f, max(f))
    q += torque / IXX * DT
    pitch += q * DT

lessons.title: The Stick Is Not the Aircraft
lessons.goal: Map a stick deflection to a body rate through an expo curve and measure the sensitivity it buys near centre.
lessons.theory:
In acro mode the stick commands a **rate**, not an attitude. Centre the stick and the aircraft holds whatever rate it has, which is zero, which is whatever attitude it happens to be in. Nothing levels it. That is the mode every racing pilot flies and the mode every autopilot uses underneath the others.

A linear map from stick to rate is unflyable at both ends at once. Enough range for a flip makes the centimetre around centre far too twitchy for a straight line. So the map is bent: `MAX_RATE * (EXPO * s ** 3 + (1.0 - EXPO) * s)`, with `EXPO` around 0.6. It is still full rate at full stick, because a cube of one is one, and it is much gentler in the middle.

The number that matters is the slope at centre, `MAX_RATE * (1.0 - EXPO)`. With a 4 rad/s maximum and 0.6 of expo, a full stick still gives 4 rad/s but the sensitivity around neutral drops from 4.0 to 1.6 rad per second per unit of stick, a factor of two and a half. That is what a pilot means by saying a machine feels locked in.

Two things this does not do. It does not change the maximum, and it does not fix a mechanically sloppy stick, because at exactly centre the curve still passes through zero with a nonzero slope. Deadband, in dr4-2, is a different tool for a different problem.

    return MAX_RATE * s

lessons.title: The Stick That Is Never Quite Centred
lessons.goal: Add a rescaled deadband to the angle mode map and show what happens without the rescale.
lessons.theory:
Angle mode maps the stick to an attitude instead of a rate. Release the stick and the aircraft returns to level on its own, which is what makes it the mode a camera flies in and the mode a beginner survives.

That creates a new problem. A physical gimbal does not return to exactly zero, and a hall sensor drifts with temperature, so a stick at rest reads 0.01 or 0.02 and the aircraft leans very slowly for the rest of the flight. The cure is a **deadband**: treat anything with `abs(s) < DEADBAND` as centre.

The naive deadband trades one defect for a worse one. Zero below the threshold and pass the raw value above it, and the output jumps by the whole threshold the moment the stick crosses it. On a 5 percent deadband and a 35 degree range that is a 1.75 degree step in commanded attitude from a millimetre of stick movement, which a pilot feels as a notch. The fix is to rescale what is left: `(s - math.copysign(DEADBAND, s)) / (1.0 - DEADBAND)`, so the curve leaves the deadband at zero and still reaches 1.0 at full stick.

Print the pair just past the edge. The naive map says 1.79 degrees, the rescaled one says 0.04, and both say 35 at full deflection. That is the whole point of a rescale: it removes a discontinuity without removing any range.
lessons.task: Implement `deadband` with the rescale and `naive_deadband` without it, then print the commanded angle from each at the deadband edge, just past it, and at full stick.
lessons.hint: Copy the sign of the stick onto the threshold before subtracting it, or the negative half of the range comes out backwards. Full stick must still map to full angle in both versions.

lessons.title: The Throttle That Means Climb Rate
lessons.goal: Turn the throttle stick into a climb rate command and measure what a mass error costs in each mode.
lessons.theory:
In manual throttle the stick is thrust. In altitude hold the stick is **climb rate**, `MAX_CLIMB * shape(stick)`, and centre means zero climb rather than a particular thrust. The controller underneath produces whatever thrust that requires: `MASS * (G + KP_VZ * (climb_sp - vz))`, a proportional loop on vertical speed sitting on top of a gravity feed forward.

The reason to prefer it is not comfort, it is robustness to being wrong about the aircraft. Hang a 150 g payload on this frame, a 10 percent mass increase, and the manual throttle that used to hover now produces 0.89 m/s squared of downward acceleration. Five seconds later the machine is 11 m lower and the pilot is the only feedback loop in the system.

The altitude hold loop sees the descent and pushes back. It does not fix it completely, because a proportional loop needs an error to produce the extra thrust, so it settles at a steady 0.33 m/s sink and loses about 1.5 m in the same five seconds. Better by a factor of seven, and still not right.

That residue is what dr5-1 removes, by learning the hover thrust in flight instead of trusting a mass written in a configuration file. Print both numbers here, because the pair is the argument for the next chapter.

lessons.title: Where the Target Comes From
lessons.goal: Latch the position target when the stick returns to centre and show the flight the alternative produces.
lessons.theory:
Position hold maps the stick to a horizontal velocity, so a centred stick means stop and stay. The interesting question is where the target comes from, and it is the one that gets answered wrong.

While the pilot is flying, `abs(stick) > STICK_EPS`, there is no target at all. The velocity command comes straight from the stick and the position loop is switched off. The moment the stick returns to centre the aircraft latches the place it is now, and on every cycle after that it keeps what it latched: `target if target is not None else x`. Clear the target on every stick input and set it exactly once on release.

The alternative is to record the position when the mode was entered and keep it. That machine flies where the pilot points it, and the moment the stick is released it turns around and flies all the way back to where the mode started, at full speed, usually toward the pilot. It is a real defect with a real history, and it is one comparison away from being obvious.

Fly the same 3 s stick input through both and print the final position. The latching version stops where it was pointed, 24 m out. The fixed target version returns to zero. Same code, same gains, one line of difference.

lessons.title: The Bump at the Switch
lessons.goal: Seed a mode with the state the previous one was producing and measure the discontinuity you avoid.
lessons.theory:
Every mode switch is a handover, and the receiving controller starts from whatever its own state says. If that state is a fresh zero and the aircraft was in the middle of holding 16 N of thrust in a 25 degree bank, the first command out of the new mode is a step, and the aircraft moves before the loop catches up.

The cure is called **bumpless transfer** and it is one assignment. When altitude hold takes over from manual throttle, seed its output with what the pilot was holding, `last_thrust if seed else MASS * G`, instead of the book hover value. When position hold takes over, seed the target with the current position, which is dr4-4 again. When any loop with an integrator takes over, preload the integrator so its total output matches what was already being commanded.

Measure the jump as `abs(first - last_thrust)` at the one instant where the word means anything: a steady hover, where the new loop has no correction of its own to make and every newton of difference is pure handover error. Carrying the payload of dr4-3 the pilot was holding 14.57 N. An unseeded altitude hold starts from the book value of 13.24 N, a step of 1.32 N in one control cycle, a tenth of the weight of the aircraft. Seeded, the step is exactly zero.

Every mode boundary in dr4-9 has a handover like this. The rule is that a mode never starts from its own defaults while the aircraft is flying, only from what the aircraft was already doing.

lessons.title: Nothing Spins Until Everything Agrees
lessons.goal: Write the arming gate as a named checklist and make it report which item refused.
lessons.theory:
Arming is the one moment where a robot is allowed to say no to its operator. Once the motors spin, a 9 inch carbon propeller at 5000 rpm is a hazard, and every check that is cheap to run before that moment is worth running.

The list on this frame: the accelerometer and gyro are calibrated, the gyro is not moving, the pack is above the arming voltage, the RC link is present, the position estimate is good enough for the mode being requested, and the throttle stick is at the bottom. Each one is a name and a boolean, and the gate is `len(failed) == 0` where the failures are `[name for name, ok in checks if not ok]`.

The names are the point. A gate that returns a single boolean gives a pilot standing in a field a machine that will not arm and no way to find out why, and the usual next step is to disable the checks. A gate that answers with `low_battery` or `gyro_moving` is a gate the pilot trusts and leaves switched on.

Print both cases, one that arms and one that does not, and print the full list of failures rather than just the first. Two problems at once is normal on a cold morning, and a checklist that stops at the first one turns a single trip to the bench into three.

lessons.title: Leaving the Ground
lessons.goal: Ramp the thrust into a takeoff, detect the liftoff from sustained vertical speed, and detect a takeoff that will not happen.
lessons.theory:
Takeoff is not a thrust setting, it is a search. The autopilot does not know the exact mass, the exact air density or how much the landing gear is stuck to wet grass, so it ramps the collective at a fixed rate and watches for the aircraft to answer.

The answer is vertical speed. Integrating `(thrust / mass - G) * DT` the aircraft stays at zero while the thrust is below its weight and starts to move above it, and the detector fires when the climb has been above a threshold for a while: `held >= LIFTOFF_HOLD`. One sample is not enough, because a gust, a bump of the leg on the ground or a noisy barometer will all produce one sample of upward speed on an aircraft that has not moved.

The other half is the failure case, and it is the half people forget. If the ramp reaches full collective and the aircraft is still on the ground, the takeoff must be abandoned and the motors stopped. Run the same routine at 4.0 kg on a frame that can push 35.6 N and it never lifts, the loop ends, and the function returns nothing rather than a time.

That is a real outcome, not an error: a battery too cold to deliver current, a payload nobody weighed, a propeller mounted upside down. The takeoff routine is often the first thing that notices, and a routine that can only report success will keep the motors spinning against the ground until something burns.

lessons.title: Three Ways to Know You Have Landed
lessons.goal: Build a landing detector on three simultaneous signals and show what each one alone gets wrong.
lessons.theory:
Landing detection decides when to cut the motors, and it is wrong in two directions. Declare a landing in the air and the aircraft falls. Fail to declare one on the ground and the machine sits there at hover thrust, tipping over on the first gust and cutting its propellers into the dirt.

No single signal is enough. Vertical speed near zero happens in a hover and at the top of a gust induced bounce. Low thrust demand happens during any commanded descent. Low attitude activity happens whenever the air is smooth. Each one alone will fire in flight on an ordinary day.

Together they will not: `thrust < LAND_THRUST and abs(vz) < LAND_VZ and tilt_activity < LAND_TILT`. On the ground the legs take the weight, so the altitude loop winds the thrust down, the vertical speed is genuinely zero and the attitude stops moving, and all three appear at once and stay. A useful diagnostic alongside the verdict is `sum(1 for x in s if x)`, the number of signals currently agreeing, because a detector sitting at two out of three for several seconds is a machine on the ground with a stuck barometer.

Run three cases: hovering steadily, floating through a gust with the vertical speed momentarily at zero, and actually down. Only the third one should be a landing, and the middle one is the case that argues for all three.
lessons.task: Implement `signals`, `agreeing` and `landed`, then print the three signal booleans, the agreement count and the verdict for a hover, a gust and a real touchdown.
lessons.hint: Build the triple as `(thrust < LAND_THRUST, abs(vz) < LAND_VZ, tilt_activity < LAND_TILT)`, with the absolute value on the vertical speed because a fast descent is not a landing either. The hover should show two signals agreeing and still not be a landing.

lessons.title: The Mode Manager
lessons.goal: Build the transition table with its per mode requirements and make every refusal come back with a reason.
lessons.theory:
The modes of this chapter are not a set, they are a graph. You cannot go from disarmed to position hold, you cannot go from land to takeoff, and you cannot enter return to home without a home point. Writing that as a table makes the aircraft's behaviour readable in one screen instead of scattered across nine handlers.

Two separate questions, in this order. Is the edge allowed at all, `wanted not in ALLOWED[current]`? And does the destination have what it needs, `[r for r in REQUIRES.get(wanted, ()) if not state[r]]`? The first is topology and never changes in flight. The second is health and changes constantly, which is why position hold is legal from altitude hold at one moment and refused at the next when the position estimate degrades.

Every refusal returns a reason. `not_allowed` means the request made no sense from here. A named requirement means the aircraft would like to and cannot yet. The autopilot logs it, the ground station shows it, and nobody has to guess why a switch on the transmitter appeared to do nothing.

And note what the manager does not do: it never refuses a **downgrade**. Land and disarm are reachable from everywhere, because the one thing a mode manager must never do is trap an aircraft in a mode it cannot leave. Chapter 8 builds the failsafe ladder on top of exactly that property.
lessons.task: Implement `request` so it checks the edge first and the requirements second, then print the outcome of five requests, including one refused for topology and one refused for a missing requirement.
lessons.hint: A refused request returns the mode the aircraft is already in, never the one it wanted, so the caller can assign the result unconditionally. The requirement check runs against the destination, not the origin.

lessons.title: Learning What a Hover Costs
lessons.goal: Learn the hover thrust in flight and remove the steady sink a mass error leaves behind.
lessons.theory:
The altitude loop of dr4-3 still sank 1.5 m under an unmodelled payload, because its feed forward was `MASS * G` and the mass in that expression came from a configuration file written before the flight. Everything about the real number changes: batteries lose 40 g of water over their life, props pick up mud, air density drops 12 percent on a hot day at 1000 m, and nobody weighs the machine again.

So measure it instead. Whenever the aircraft is genuinely holding height, `abs(vz) < LEARN_VZ and climb_sp == 0.0`, the thrust it is currently commanding **is** the hover thrust, and a slow filter can adopt it: `hover_thrust + (thrust_cmd - hover_thrust) * (DT / TAU_LEARN)`. Ten seconds of time constant is right. Fast enough to catch a payload release, slow enough that it never chases a gust.

The gate matters as much as the filter, and its threshold has to be wider than the error it is meant to cure. Learn while climbing and the filter adopts a climbing thrust and the aircraft runs away upward, so the gate has to be tight. Set it tighter than the steady sink the payload causes, 0.33 m/s, and the gate never opens at all: the aircraft sinks forever waiting for a hover it is not allowed to have. Half a metre per second is the compromise.

Run the payload case again over forty seconds with learning on. The estimate walks from 13.24 N up to 14.55 against a true 14.57, and the sink dies with it: 0.006 m/s left instead of 0.327. The uncorrected machine is 13 m low and still going down at the same rate it started; the learner stops at 3.2 m and stays there. Note what is not claimed here, since there is no altitude loop in this experiment: the aircraft does not climb back. It stops falling.

lessons.title: Down Is Not Up Backwards
lessons.goal: Compute the vertical acceleration available in each direction and the descent rates the air will not allow.
lessons.theory:
A multirotor climbs and descends with entirely different physics, and treating the vertical axis as symmetric is how a machine ends up falling out of its own downwash.

The first asymmetry is thrust. Upward the aircraft has everything above the weight, `(MAX_TOTAL - MASS * G) / MASS`, which is 16.6 m/s squared on this frame, over one and a half g. Downward it can only reduce thrust to the idle floor of dr1-8, `(MIN_TOTAL - MASS * G) / MASS`, so the strongest downward acceleration is 8.8 m/s squared and it can never exceed gravity. A quadrotor cannot dive.

The second asymmetry is the air, and it bites earlier. Descend vertically at somewhere between half and one and a half times the rotor's own induced velocity and the machine settles into the ring of turbulent air it just pushed down. That is the **vortex ring state**: the propellers are working in their own wake, thrust collapses, and adding throttle makes it worse because it makes the ring stronger. With an induced velocity of 5.74 m/s on this frame the dangerous band is `0.5 * INDUCED_VELOCITY <= rate <= 1.5 * INDUCED_VELOCITY`, 2.9 to 8.6 m/s straight down.

So the descent limit in the parameter file is 2.5 m/s, not because the motors cannot do more but because the air will not let them. The way out of a vortex ring is sideways, which is why every descent profile in chapter 8 has forward speed in it.

lessons.title: The Metre the Wind Takes
lessons.goal: Predict the steady position offset a proportional cascade leaves under a constant force, and confirm it in flight.
lessons.theory:
Put the aircraft of chapter 3 in a steady 3 N breeze and it will hold position badly, in a very specific and predictable way. It ends up sitting downwind of its target and staying there, perfectly stable, at a fixed distance.

The distance follows from the loop having nothing but proportional terms. In the steady state the velocity is zero, so the acceleration command is `KP_VEL * KP_POS * error`, and it has to equal the disturbance acceleration to balance it. Solve for the error and it is `disturbance / (MASS * KP_POS * KP_VEL)`, which at 3 N with gains of 1.0 and 2.0 is 1.11 m. Every metre of that offset is the loop paying for the wind with position error, because position error is the only currency it has.

You can attack it three ways and only one of them is right. Raising the gains shrinks the offset in proportion and amplifies estimator noise by the same factor, which is dr5-8. Accepting it makes a machine that cannot hold a spot in any wind at all. Adding an integrator removes it entirely, which is dr5-4.

lessons.title: The Integrator Is an Anemometer
lessons.goal: Add the integral term, watch it converge on the disturbance, and read the wind out of it.
lessons.theory:
An integral term removes the offset of dr5-3, which is the usual reason to add one. On an aircraft it does something more useful: it **becomes a measurement**.

Think about where it settles. At equilibrium the position error is zero, so every proportional term is zero, and the only thing left producing the acceleration that balances the wind is the integrator. Its converged value is therefore exactly the disturbance acceleration, and `MASS * integral` is the disturbance force in newtons. The aircraft has weighed the wind using nothing but its own control loop, and chapter 6 uses that number to decide whether it can still get home.

Update it as `integral + KI_VEL * error * DT`, and freeze it when the tilt limiter of dr2-9 is active. That guard is not about elegance. A machine at maximum tilt is not going to move whatever the integrator says, so integrating there fills it with a number that has to be unwound afterwards, and the aircraft overshoots the moment the wind drops.

Run it against a 3 N disturbance. The integrator converges on minus 2.222 m/s squared, the estimated force lands on minus 3.0 N against a true plus 3.0, and the position error goes to zero instead of the 1.11 m of dr5-3. The sign is not a bug and it is not a detail: the integrator holds the acceleration that **cancels** the wind, so the force it reports is the one the aircraft is applying and the wind is the negative of it. One term, two results.

lessons.title: The Cushion Near the Floor
lessons.goal: Model ground effect and show why an aircraft descending on a fixed thrust refuses to touch down.
lessons.theory:
Within about one rotor radius of the ground the downwash cannot get out of the way, and the rotor gets more thrust for the same power. The standard model is a multiplier, `1.0 / (1.0 - (PROP_RADIUS / (4.0 * height)) ** 2)`, and with a 0.114 m radius it is worth 6.7 percent at one radius up, 1.6 percent at one diameter, and essentially nothing above half a metre.

Six percent does not sound like much until you notice that it appears exactly where the aircraft is trying to make a controlled contact with a hard object. The thrust needed to hover is `MASS * G / factor`, so a machine descending at constant commanded thrust decelerates on its own as it enters the cushion, floats, and drifts sideways while it does. Every pilot has seen it and half of them think the machine is fighting them.

There is a second effect and it is the reason landings go wrong rather than merely slowly. Ground effect is not uniform: over uneven ground, or with one side of the aircraft over a step or a kerb, one pair of rotors gets the cushion and the other does not, so the machine gets a rolling moment out of nowhere at the worst possible moment.

The landing detector of dr4-8 is what saves this. It watches the commanded thrust rather than the height, and the commanded thrust in ground effect goes **down**, so the detector fires earlier rather than later, which is the right direction to be wrong in.

lessons.title: How Good Is This Hover
lessons.goal: Measure hover quality as an RMS radius over a window and compare two gain settings against a spec.
lessons.theory:
Hover quality has to be a number or it is an opinion. The number is the root mean square radius over a window: `math.sqrt(sum(r * r for r in radii) / len(radii))`, taken over the last thirty seconds of a stationary hold. Manufacturers quote it as a positioning accuracy and it is the only honest way to compare two tunings.

Use the RMS and not the maximum. One gust puts a 60 cm spike in any log and the maximum reports that spike forever, so it measures the weather rather than the aircraft. The RMS reports what the machine did for most of the window, and a spec of `rms <= HOVER_SPEC` at 0.30 m is what this frame should manage in still air.

Feed the same seeded turbulence into two position gains and read the pair. Under a 4 N root mean square buffeting, roughly a third of the weight of the aircraft, the gentle gain of 0.15 wanders 0.63 m and misses the spec by a factor of two. The firm gain of 1.0 holds 0.19 m and passes. Neither number means anything without the other, because the input is a random sequence and the only fair comparison is the same sequence through both.

Seed it, always. An unseeded run gives a different verdict each time it is executed, and a metric whose answer changes when nothing changed is not a metric.

lessons.title: The Payload That Leaves
lessons.goal: Drop 300 g in mid flight and measure the height excursion and the time the learned hover thrust needs to recover.
lessons.theory:
A delivery drone releasing a package, a sprayer emptying a tank, a machine picking something up: the mass changes while the loop is closed, and the learned hover thrust of dr5-1 is suddenly wrong by exactly the weight that left.

Release 300 g and the aircraft is instantly 2.94 N over thrusted. It accelerates upward at 2.2 m/s squared until the vertical loop catches it, then sits 0.70 m high while the slow learner walks the hover estimate back down. Two numbers describe the whole event: the excursion, `max(abs(h) for h in trace)`, and the recovery time, which is the last moment the aircraft was outside the acceptance band and not the first moment it was inside it.

That definition is worth stopping on. Written as the first moment inside the band, a trace that dips through the band on its way to a large overshoot reports a recovery it never made. Written as the last moment outside it, scanning backwards with `if abs(trace[i]) > band:`, no excursion after that instant can hide.

The tuning tension shows up here, and the recovery time is where you read it: 34 s to get back inside 5 cm. The ten second learning time constant that keeps gusts out of the estimate is also half a minute of hanging high after a release. Fast delivery machines gate the learner on a discrete event instead, and reset the estimate the moment the release actuator fires, because they know the mass changed and by how much.

lessons.title: The Noise You Amplify
lessons.goal: Feed a noisy position estimate into two gains and measure the tilt activity each one produces.
lessons.theory:
Raising the position gain shrinks the wind offset of dr5-3 in exact proportion. It also multiplies whatever noise is on the position estimate by the same factor, and turns it into tilt commands, and tilt commands into motor current.

The chain is short and mechanical. The loop does not see `x`, it sees `KP_POS * (target - (x + noise))`, and the noise term goes straight through the velocity stage into an acceleration and then into an angle. With 4 cm of GPS noise on the estimate, a gain of 0.6 produces a fraction of a degree of tilt activity and a gain of 2.5 produces four times as much, on an aircraft that is not moving at all.

Measure it as an RMS of the commanded tilt, `math.sqrt(sum(t * t for t in tilts) / len(tilts))`, in degrees. It is a proxy for something you cannot easily simulate: motors that never stop correcting, ESCs that run hot, a flight time shorter than the datasheet, and a video feed with a shimmer in it that nobody can trace.

So the position gain has a good reason to go up and a good reason to go down, and both reasons are in this chapter. The right answer depends on how noisy the estimate is, which is why a machine with an optical flow sensor over a textured floor can be tuned far more firmly than the same machine on satellite navigation alone.

lessons.title: The Hover Module
lessons.goal: Assemble learned hover thrust, the integral wind estimate and the quality metric into one holding controller.
lessons.theory:
The hover controller is now four pieces that have to run together: the learned hover thrust of dr5-1, the position latch of dr4-4, the integral term of dr5-4 with its freeze, and the quality metric of dr5-6 reporting on all of it.

The order inside one cycle is fixed. Read the estimate. Update the position error against the latched target. Run the velocity loop with its integral. Ask for a tilt, and if the tilt limiter bites, tell the integrator not to accumulate this cycle. Run the vertical loop on the learned hover thrust. Update the learner only if this cycle was genuinely a hover. Record the radius for the metric.

What comes out is not just a command, it is a report: the hold radius, the wind the integrator has weighed, `MASS * integral`, and whether the aircraft is meeting its own specification right now. Every one of those three feeds something later. Chapter 6 uses the wind estimate to decide if the machine can still make progress upwind, chapter 8 uses it to price the trip home, and the quality flag is what a mission planner should be looking at before it commits to a long leg.

Run it in a 4 N crosswind. The hold radius stays inside the 0.30 m specification, the wind estimate lands within a few percent of the truth, and the aircraft is holding a position it would have been more than a metre away from at the end of chapter 3.

TAU_LEARN = 10.0
LEARN_VZ = 0.20

    x, v, integral, vz, hover_thrust = state
    v_sp = KP_POS * (0.0 - x)
    error = v_sp - v
    a_cmd = KP_VEL * error + integral
    tilt = math.atan2(a_cmd, G)
    tilt_limited = abs(tilt) > MAX_TILT

    v += a * DT
    x += v * DT
    vz += (thrust / MASS - G) * DT
    return (x, v, integral, vz, hover_thrust)
