lessons.title: The Push You Cannot See
lessons.goal: Compute the drag force a steady wind applies and the lean the aircraft has to hold to stay put.
lessons.theory:
Wind does not push an aircraft sideways because it is windy. It pushes because the airframe is a bluff body moving through air at the wind speed, and the force is `DRAG_K * airspeed * airspeed`, with `DRAG_K` collecting half the air density, the drag coefficient and the frontal area. On this frame, with a 1.1 coefficient over 0.09 square metres in sea level air, `DRAG_K` is 0.0606 N per squared metre per second.

The square is what makes wind dangerous rather than annoying. Five metres per second costs 1.5 N, a ninth of the weight. Ten costs 6.1 N, and fifteen costs 13.6 N, which is more than the aircraft weighs. Doubling the wind quadruples the problem, so a machine that is comfortable in a breeze can be entirely out of options in what the forecast calls a fresh wind.

To stay over a point the aircraft has to produce an equal and opposite horizontal force, which from dr0-5 means leaning by `math.atan2(drag_force(wind), MASS * G)`. At 10 m/s that is 24.6 degrees of permanent lean, most of the 35 degree limit, held for as long as the wind blows, with nothing left for a gust on top.

Note where that lean comes from. Nobody commands it. It is the integrator of dr5-4 finding it, one small increment at a time, which is why the integral term is the difference between a machine that holds a spot in wind and one that gets blown away while looking perfectly stable.

lessons.title: The Wind That Wins
lessons.goal: Invert the tilt limit into a maximum holdable wind and set an operating margin under it.
lessons.theory:
There is a wind speed above which this aircraft cannot hold a position, and it is a property of the airframe, not of the tuning. At the tilt limit the horizontal force available is `MASS * G * math.tan(MAX_TILT)`, 9.27 N at 35 degrees. Set that equal to the drag and solve: `math.sqrt(MASS * G * math.tan(max_tilt) / DRAG_K)`, 12.4 m/s.

Above it the machine leans as far as it is allowed, produces less force than the air is applying, and travels downwind at an increasing speed while its attitude controller reports perfect health. Nothing is broken. It simply loses, and the log will show a saturated tilt and a position error that grows without limit, which is the signature to recognise.

Never operate at the limit. The number that goes in the flight plan is the margin, `WIND_MARGIN * max_wind`, at 0.7 or so, which puts this frame at 8.7 m/s. The three metres per second you gave away buy the authority to fight a gust, to make progress upwind instead of merely holding, and to survive a wind that is stronger at altitude than it was on the ground, which is dr6-8.

Raising the tilt limit to 45 degrees buys 14.7 m/s, and costs 41 percent more thrust to hold altitude while leaning, from dr3-6. On a machine with a thrust to weight of 2.7 that trade is available. On a heavy lifter at 1.6 it is not, which is why big camera drones are grounded by wind that a racing quad does not notice.

lessons.title: Airspeed Is the Only Speed the Air Knows
lessons.goal: Separate airspeed from ground speed and compute how fast the aircraft can still make progress upwind.
lessons.theory:
The autopilot works in ground coordinates. The air does not. Drag is produced by `airspeed = ground_speed + wind` when flying into the wind, and the two numbers are only equal on a still day, which is the day nobody has a problem.

Hovering over a point in a 10 m/s wind, the ground speed is zero and the airspeed is 10. The aircraft is flying, hard, and burning the power to prove it. Fly upwind on top of that and the airspeed goes up further, so the drag goes up as the square of it, which is why the last few metres per second of upwind progress are so expensive.

Solve for what is left. At the tilt limit the available force is fixed, so the airspeed is capped at 12.4 m/s from dr6-2, and the best upwind ground speed is `max_airspeed() - wind`. In a 10 m/s wind that is 2.4 m/s of progress, a crawl. In a 12.4 m/s wind it is zero, and above that the number goes negative, which is the aircraft reporting honestly that it is losing ground at full effort.

This is the calculation that decides whether a return to home is a plan or a wish, and chapter 8 puts it in front of the failsafe. A machine 800 m out in a 10 m/s headwind needs 335 seconds to get back, not the 100 the still air arithmetic promises, and the battery does not care which number was in the flight plan.

lessons.title: The Gust That Arrives All At Once
lessons.goal: Hit the position hold with a step change in wind and measure the excursion and the recovery.
lessons.theory:
A steady wind is a solved problem after dr5-4. A gust is a different question, because the integrator that solves the steady case is deliberately slow and a gust is not.

Step the wind from nothing to 8 m/s in one sample and watch the sequence. The drag appears immediately, 3.9 N of it. The proportional terms respond in proportion to an error that does not exist yet, so for the first fraction of a second nothing useful happens and the aircraft simply accelerates downwind. The error builds, the proportional terms bite, and the machine slows and stops, displaced. Only then does the integrator walk the lean in and bring it back.

Two numbers, and they come from different parts of the loop. The excursion, `max(abs(x) for x in trace)`, is set by the proportional gains and the mass. The recovery time is set by the integral gain, and it is the last moment the aircraft was outside the band, using the backwards scan of dr5-7 for the same reason as before.

Which explains why gust performance and noise performance pull in opposite directions, as dr5-8 showed. Everything that makes the excursion smaller makes the aircraft twitchier on a calm day. The way out is not a better gain, it is a faster measurement, and a machine with a forward facing airspeed sensor can react to a gust before it has moved at all.

lessons.title: Reading the Wind Off the Controller
lessons.goal: Turn the converged integral term into a wind speed and direction, and check it against the truth.
lessons.theory:
The aircraft has an anemometer and it did not cost anything. From dr5-4 the converged integrator holds the acceleration that cancels the disturbance, so `MASS * abs(integral)` is the force the air is applying, and dr6-1 inverts to a speed: `math.sqrt(force / DRAG_K)`.

Three things make this estimate honest. It only means anything once the integrator has converged, so gate it on the aircraft having held position for several seconds. It measures the **total** disturbance, so a dragging tether or an iced up arm shows up as wind that is not there, which is a feature if you read it as "something is pushing on me" rather than "the weather is". And it is a two component vector, so the direction comes free from the two horizontal integrators, negated because they hold the correction and not its cause: `math.degrees(math.atan2(-integral_y, -integral_x))`.

Check it against the truth in simulation and the error is a fraction of a percent, because the same drag model generates the disturbance and interprets it. In the air it is worse, since the real drag coefficient changes with the tilt angle and with whether the machine is carrying anything, and 15 percent is a good day.

Fifteen percent is plenty. Every decision this estimate feeds is a threshold: can I hold, can I make progress upwind, do I have the energy to get home. None of them needs three digits, and all of them are worthless without any number at all.

lessons.title: Out and Back Is Not Twice One Way
lessons.goal: Compute the round trip time in wind and find the wind at which the outbound leg never finishes.
lessons.theory:
Intuition says a headwind out and a tailwind back cancel out. They do not, and the reason is that you spend a long time in the slow half and very little in the fast half.

Fly 200 m out and back at an 8 m/s airspeed. In still air the trip takes `distance / ground` twice over, 50 s. In a 4 m/s wind the outbound leg runs at 4 m/s of ground speed and takes 50 s on its own, while the return runs at 12 and takes 16.7, for 66.7 s total. A third longer, from a wind half the cruise speed. The general shape is that the round trip time grows without limit as the wind approaches the airspeed, and it never gets shorter.

At 8 m/s of wind the outbound ground speed is zero and the leg never finishes at all, so the function returns nothing rather than a division by zero or a negative time. That is the honest answer and the caller has to handle it, exactly as in the failed takeoff of dr4-7.

Note the escape, though: the aircraft is not stuck at its cruise airspeed. The 12.4 m/s of dr6-3 is still available, so the leg can be flown at full tilt into an 8 m/s wind at 4.4 m/s of ground speed. It costs far more energy per metre, and chapter 7 prices it. This is the moment where the wind chapter and the battery chapter meet, and the answer is not always that the aircraft can afford it.

lessons.title: Wind Is Not a Constant
lessons.goal: Drive the hold with correlated turbulence and compare it against a steady wind of the same average.
lessons.theory:
Real wind is a mean with a rough surface on it, and the roughness has memory: a gust lasts a second or two rather than one control cycle. White noise is the wrong model, because a controller filters it out for free and the simulation flatters itself.

The cheap correct model is a first order process around the mean: `MEAN_WIND + (w - MEAN_WIND) * decay() + GUST_SIGMA * noise`, where the decay is `math.exp(-DT / TAU_GUST)`, the fraction of the current deviation that survives one step. Two seconds of correlation and a 2 m/s deviation is an ordinary day in open country. It looks like wind on a plot, and more importantly it sits in the frequency band the position loop cannot reject.

Run the same aircraft against a steady 8 m/s and against turbulence averaging 8 m/s. The steady case settles to a hold radius near zero, because the integrator finds the lean and holds it. The turbulent case does not settle at all, and the hold radius is the whole answer to how good the machine is on that day.

That gap is why hover specifications carry a wind condition and why a machine tested indoors will disappoint outdoors even with the same firmware. Seed the noise, run both from the same generator, and the comparison is meaningful. Leave it unseeded and you have a metric that argues with itself.

lessons.title: The Wind Upstairs
lessons.goal: Model the wind gradient with height and decide what a climb costs before a long leg.
lessons.theory:
The wind at 100 m is not the wind at the launch site, and the difference is large enough to change a decision. Friction with the ground slows the lowest layer of the atmosphere, and the standard engineering model is a power law: `reference * (height / REFERENCE_HEIGHT) ** alpha`, with an exponent near 0.14 over open ground and 0.25 or more over a town.

Measure 8 m/s at 10 m over a field and the same air is moving at 11.0 m/s at 100 m. Over a built up area, where the exponent is larger, the surface reading is lower but the gradient is steeper and the number at height is much the same. Either way the machine that took off comfortably inside its 8.7 m/s margin from dr6-2 is outside it once it climbs to a return altitude.

So the return altitude of chapter 8 is a real trade rather than a safety default. Higher means clearing obstacles and finding a stronger tailwind if the wind happens to be going your way, and it means a stronger headwind if it is not, at exactly the moment the battery is low.

Print the profile and then check each height with `w > OPERATING_LIMIT` against the margin of dr6-2. The two heights that pass and the one that does not are the flight plan, and this is the last piece the wind monitor of dr6-9 needs.

The estimate of dr6-5 is only worth having if something acts on it. That something is a monitor with four levels, `ORDER` from `ok` through `caution` and `return` to `land`, and two rules about how it moves between them.

The first rule is escalation only: `ORDER.index(level) > ORDER.index(current)`. lessons.title: What a Hover Costs
lessons.goal: Compute the induced velocity and the electrical power a hover consumes on this airframe.
lessons.theory:
A ground robot at rest costs nothing. An aerial one at rest costs everything it has, and the bill comes from momentum theory: to hold itself up the rotor has to throw air downward, and the power is the thrust times the speed it throws it at.

That speed is the **induced velocity**, `math.sqrt(thrust / (2.0 * RHO * DISK_AREA))`, with `DISK_AREA` the total swept area of all four rotors, 0.164 square metres here. At the 13.24 N this frame weighs, the air leaves at 5.74 m/s and the ideal power is 76 W. Notice what the disk area does: it sits under a square root in the denominator, so a bigger propeller is cheaper to hover on. This is the whole reason endurance machines have absurd propellers.

Ideal is not real. A rotor converts shaft power to thrust with a figure of merit around 0.65, and the motor and ESC together deliver about 0.80 of the electrical power as shaft power, so what the battery actually pays is `thrust * induced_velocity(thrust) / (FIGURE_OF_MERIT * DRIVE_EFFICIENCY)`, 146 W.

Hold on to the shape of that expression, because it is the reason everything in this chapter is nonlinear. Power goes as thrust times the square root of thrust, so it climbs with the 1.5 power of weight. Ten percent heavier is fifteen percent more power, and there is no tuning, no firmware and no propeller that changes the exponent.

lessons.title: Minutes, Not Watt Hours

The pack on this frame is a 4S 5.2 Ah lithium polymer, which at a 14.8 V nominal is 77 Wh of stored energy. At the 146 W of dr7-1 that would be 31 minutes of hovering, and anyone who plans a 31 minute flight will land by parachute.

lessons.title: The Voltage That Runs Away From You
lessons.goal: Solve the loaded pack voltage against its own internal resistance and read the thrust it can still produce.
lessons.theory:
A battery quoted at 16.0 V is 16.0 V with nothing attached. Pull current through it and the internal resistance takes its cut, and the aircraft never sees the number on the label.

The awkward part is that the sag depends on the current and the current depends on the voltage, so there is no closed form to copy. lessons.title: What a Kilogram Costs
lessons.goal: Price a payload in power and in flight minutes, and show the exponent that makes it worse than linear.
lessons.theory:
Ask what a 300 g camera costs on a 1.35 kg aircraft and the intuitive answer is 22 percent, because that is how much heavier it is. The real answer is 35 percent of the power and a quarter of the flight time, and the gap between those numbers is the whole reason aerial engineering is conservative about mass.

The exponent comes straight out of dr7-1. Thrust has to equal weight, induced velocity goes as the square root of thrust, and power is the product, so power goes as weight to the 1.5. Then the flight time falls twice over, because the aircraft is spending faster out of the same pack: 25.3 minutes becomes 18.7. Every gram counts twice, which is why the answer to a mount that could be milled thinner is usually yes.

Print the whole table, four payloads, three columns. It is the single most useful piece of paper in an aerial project, because it converts an argument about a component into an argument about minutes, and minutes are what the mission is specified in.

lessons.goal: Sweep the pack mass against endurance and find the point where more battery stops helping.
lessons.theory:
More battery is more energy and also more weight, and weight costs power at the 1.5 exponent of dr7-4. Somewhere those two curves cross, and past that point every extra cell you bolt on makes the aircraft fly for less time than it did before.

Write it out. The energy is `pack_mass * SPECIFIC_ENERGY`, about 180 Wh per kilogram for a good lithium polymer, and the power is set by the total of frame plus pack. On this frame, 0.94 kg without its battery, that means a 1.88 kg pack, a 2.8 kg aircraft, and 36.8 minutes against the 23.9 the real 0.4 kg pack delivers. This is also the input to everything that follows. The return trigger of dr7-7 and the supervisor of dr7-9 both need to know how much is left right now, not how much a healthy pack would have left after a nominal flight.

lessons.title: The Energy to Get Home
lessons.goal: Price the return leg in watt hours against the wind and decide when the aircraft must turn around.
lessons.theory:
The decision to come back is not about how much battery is left. It is about how much is left compared to what the trip home costs from **here**, in **this** wind, and that second number moves during the flight.

Build it from parts you already have. The ground speed upwind is `max_airspeed() - wind` from dr6-3, so the time is `distance / upwind_ground_speed(wind)`, and the power is the leaning power of dr7-6 at that airspeed. Multiply, add a fixed allowance for the descent and landing, and you have the cost of going home.

Run it at 400 m out. In still air the return costs 2.6 Wh and takes 32 s. In a 6 m/s headwind it costs 4.2 Wh and takes a minute. In a 10 m/s headwind it costs 10.0 Wh and takes 169 s, a sixth of the whole usable pack, because the aircraft crawls home at 2.4 m/s while burning more power than a hover to do it. The distance did not change. The wind did.

Then trigger on `needed * RESERVE_FACTOR`, with the factor at 1.3 or so, because the estimate is built on a drag model and a wind estimate that are both approximate and the consequence of being wrong is not a late landing. An aircraft that turns back at exactly the computed cost lands short, every time it is windier than the model thought.

lessons.title: The Margin That Drains With the Pack
lessons.goal: Track the thrust to weight ratio down the discharge curve and find the voltage where a laden aircraft loses its authority.
lessons.theory:
Everything chapter 1 computed about mixer authority assumed a fixed maximum thrust. From dr7-3 that maximum falls with the pack, so the aircraft ends its flight with much less margin than it began with, and the machine that was easy to fly at takeoff is not the machine that is landing.

Follow the ratio down: `max_thrust_at(v) / weight`, computed at the loaded voltage for the power the aircraft is actually drawing. Unladen it is comfortable throughout, from 3.4 at a fresh 16.8 V to 2.0 at a flat 13.2. Put the 600 g payload of dr7-4 on it and the same sweep starts at 2.27 and passes below a 1.5 floor at 13.6 V, with plenty of nominal capacity still in the pack.

Below that floor the aircraft is still flying, and the mixer authority of dr1-8 has collapsed with the thrust, the climb rate of dr5-2 has gone, and a gust that needs a fast correction gets a slow one. That is where laden machines are lost, not at zero volts.

So the low battery threshold is not a property of the battery. Set it at `twr < MIN_TWR` on the current mass and the current draw, and the same aircraft will warn at 13.2 V empty and at 13.6 V loaded, which is exactly the behaviour you want and exactly what a fixed voltage threshold cannot do.

lessons.title: The Energy Supervisor
lessons.goal: Combine the remaining energy, the return cost and the thrust margin into one latched advisory that can refuse to stay out.
lessons.theory:
Three separate measurements, one decision. The integrated energy of dr7-6 says what is left. The return cost of dr7-7 says what going home is worth right now. The margin of dr7-8 says whether the aircraft still has the authority to fly at all. The supervisor turns them into a level and the level never goes backwards.

The ladder is `ENERGY_ORDER`, `nominal` to `warn` to `return` to `land_now`. `warn` fires at twice the return cost, because a pilot who is told at exactly the trigger has no time to finish anything. `return` fires at `remaining <= needed * RETURN_FACTOR`, the reserve rule of dr7-7. `land_now` fires when either the reserve is gone entirely or the thrust margin is below its floor, since neither of those can be solved by flying further.

Latching is what makes it usable, `ENERGY_ORDER.index(level) > ENERGY_ORDER.index(current)`. Remaining energy only ever falls, so latching the energy levels is nearly free, but the return cost jumps around with the wind estimate, and without the latch a machine that decided to come home in a gust changes its mind in the lull two seconds later. That is the same failure as dr6-9 and it has the same cure.

Run the sequence and read both columns. The aircraft asks for `nominal` twice, then `warn`, then `return` as the cost climbs, then `nominal` again when the wind eases and the return gets cheap, and finally `land_now` when the thrust margin collapses. The supervisor column refuses that fifth reading and stays at `return`, which is the latch doing its job. The first two rows stay at `nominal` in both columns, which is the proof that the level is genuinely computed rather than latched into existence by the first evaluation.

lessons.title: The Point You Are Allowed to Call Home
lessons.goal: Set the home point under explicit conditions and refuse every request that does not meet them.
lessons.theory:
Return to home is only as good as the home. Every serious incident report that begins with an aircraft flying confidently into a hedge ends with a home point that was recorded before the position estimate had settled.

So home is not recorded when the operator presses a button. It is recorded once, at arming, and only if the estimate is worth trusting: refuse while `state["accuracy_m"] > HOME_ACCURACY` at 2.5 m, and refuse while `state["satellites"] < MIN_SATELLITES` at eight. A machine that armed on six satellites in a car park has a home point somewhere in the next street, and it will fly there with total confidence.

Then refuse to move it. Once set, a request to reset home mid flight comes back `already_set`, because the operator is 400 m away and the aircraft is the thing that knows where it took off from. Automatic home updates during flight are a feature on some autopilots and they are the reason some aircraft return to the last place they had a good fix rather than the place the pilot is standing.

Every refusal comes back with a name, exactly as in the arming gate of dr4-6. `accuracy`, `satellites`, `already_set`. A ground station showing "home not set: satellites" is a thirty second wait. A ground station showing nothing is a flight nobody should start.

lessons.goal: Choose a return altitude from the obstacles below and check the wind that lives up there.
lessons.theory:
The default answer is to climb before returning, and it is right for the reason everyone gives: the aircraft does not know what is between it and home, so it goes over. The altitude is `max(obstacles) + CLEARANCE`, the tallest thing on the route plus a margin, 15 m here.

It is not right for the reason nobody mentions. From dr6-8 the wind gets stronger with height, so the return altitude that clears the trees may be in air the aircraft cannot make progress through. Check it with the power law itself, `reference * (height / REFERENCE_HEIGHT) ** alpha`, at the chosen altitude, against the operating margin of dr6-2. A 7.5 m/s wind measured at 10 m is 9.3 m/s at the 46 m these obstacles demand, past the 8.66 m/s margin. lessons.title: The Distance You Cannot Come Back From

lessons.theory:
Range is usually quoted as how far a machine can fly. The number that matters is half that, and it moves with the weather: how far it can be and still get back.

lessons.title: Losing the Pilot
lessons.goal: Debounce the radio link so a dropped frame is not a failsafe and a real loss still is.
lessons.theory:
A 2.4 GHz radio link drops frames. It drops them when the aircraft turns and puts its own battery between the antennas, when a car goes past, and when the transmitter is held at the wrong angle. A failsafe that fires on one missing frame will fire on every flight, and the standard response to that is to switch the failsafe off, which is how a machine ends up with no failsafe at all.

Count instead of deciding. Each frame either resets the counter or increases it, `0 if frame_ok else missing + 1`, and the link is declared lost only when `missing * FRAME_MS >= LOSS_MS`, with frames every 20 ms and a one second threshold. Fifty consecutive misses is not a car going past.

The counter has to reset on any good frame, not decay slowly. A link that delivers one frame in three is unusable and a decaying counter will hover just under the threshold forever, which produces the worst possible outcome: an aircraft that is not being controlled and is not in failsafe either. Either the pilot is there or they are not.

Run the sequence and watch the second gap trip it. Then watch the link come back afterwards: the counter resets and the flag clears, and it is the arbiter of dr8-9, not this function, that decides whether the aircraft is allowed to un-failsafe. lessons.title: Flying Blind on a Budget
lessons.goal: Grow the position uncertainty after a navigation loss and decide how long the aircraft may keep going.
lessons.theory:
When the position estimate dies, the aircraft does not stop knowing where it is. It starts knowing worse, at a predictable rate, and the useful question is how many seconds of that it can afford before the answer is not worth flying on.

Model it as a straight line: `accuracy0 + DRIFT_RATE * t`. With attitude and an accelerometer alone, half a metre per second of growth is optimistic and a metre is realistic on a windy day, because the drift comes from an unknown wind pushing an aircraft that thinks it is stationary. Start from a 1 m fix at a metre a second and the estimate is worth ten metres after nine seconds.

Set a radius that means something and land at it. `sigma >= SAFE_RADIUS`, with the radius chosen from what is around: 10 m over a field, 3 m over a car park. Then the time budget is the number of seconds until that happens, and the correct action at the end of it is to descend where the aircraft is, not to keep flying toward a home point it can no longer find.

This is the failure where returning home is the wrong answer, and it is the one people get wrong because return to home is the reflex for everything else. An aircraft with no position estimate cannot navigate to a coordinate. It can hold attitude and it can come down slowly, and it should do exactly that while it still knows roughly where it is.

lessons.title: Three Rotors and a Spin
lessons.goal: Work out what a quadrotor can still do with one motor dead and when that is not enough.
lessons.theory:
A quadrotor with a dead rotor cannot balance its torques with the remaining three. The standard survivable answer is to shut down the **opposite** rotor as well and fly on one diagonal: two rotors, both spinning the same way, so the aircraft yaws continuously and nobody can stop it. Roll and pitch are still controllable in the spinning frame, and a controlled spinning descent is a landing.

What decides whether that is a landing or a fall is one ratio. The thrust available is `(ROTORS - 2) * MAX_THRUST_PER_MOTOR`, 17.8 N on this frame, against a weight of 13.2. The margin is 1.35, thin but real, and the aircraft can hold altitude and come down under control.

Put the 600 g payload of dr7-4 on the same machine and the weight is 19.1 N against the same 17.8. The ratio is 0.93 and there is no arrangement of two rotors that holds it up. The best remaining outcome is the slowest possible descent, `thrust / mass - G`, which is minus 0.67 m/s squared, so the aircraft accelerates downward gently and arrives at 8.2 m/s from 50 m. That is a crash, and it is a much better crash than a tumble.

Which is the real lesson of this chapter. The failsafe does not choose between working and failing, it chooses the best available outcome, and the ratio above is what tells you which outcomes are still on the table. On a hexarotor the same arithmetic gives 2.7 and a normal landing, which is what people are paying for when they buy six arms.

lessons.title: The Fence That Has to Brake in Time
lessons.goal: Limit the speed by the distance left to the fence and show what a tailwind does to the margin.
lessons.theory:
A geofence written as a test on position is a fence the aircraft crosses. By the time the position is outside, the machine is still doing 8 m/s and needs the 7.3 m of dr3-3 to stop, so the breach happens whatever the code does next.

A fence that works limits the speed on the way in. The largest speed from which the aircraft can still stop before the line is `math.sqrt(2.0 * MAX_ACCEL * max(0.0, distance - MARGIN))`, the braking formula solved for speed, with a margin so the stop finishes inside the fence rather than exactly on it. At 40 m out it allows 23 m/s and at 10 m it still allows 11, both more than the 8 m/s this aircraft cruises at, so nothing happens at all. At 3 m it allows 5.2 and the machine slows. Inside the 1 m margin it allows nothing. The aircraft slides to a stop against an invisible wall and never sets off an alarm.

Wind changes the arithmetic and the code has to see it. Downwind the aircraft brakes against a tailwind, so the effective deceleration is lower and every allowance in the table is optimistic. The honest version subtracts the wind drag from the available acceleration before taking the root, `MAX_ACCEL - DRAG_K * wind * wind / MASS`, and in an 8 m/s tailwind the allowance at 10 m drops from 11.1 to 8.5 and at 3 m from 5.2 to 4.0.

The general shape is worth taking away from this chapter. A limit that is checked is a limit that gets crossed. A limit that shapes the command upstream is a limit the aircraft cannot reach, and the failsafe never has to fire at all.

lessons.title: The Failsafe Arbiter
lessons.goal: Map every failure to an action, take the worst of the ones that are active, and never allow the result to relax.
lessons.theory:
Failures arrive together. A pack that has been pushed hard is a pack that sags, and a sagging pack browns out a receiver, so low battery and link loss show up in the same second and both want to be handled. The arbiter is the thing that decides what actually happens.

Two pieces. `ACTION_FOR` maps each failure to the action it deserves on its own: link loss to `return`, low battery to `return`, geofence breach to `return`, position loss to `land`, motor failure to `land`, critical battery to `land`. Then the arbiter takes the worst of the active ones, `max(actions, key=ACTION_ORDER.index)`, using an ordering from `continue` through `return` to `land` and finally `terminate`.

Note which way the mapping goes for position loss. It is not the most alarming failure on the list and it gets the second most severe action, because from dr8-5 an aircraft with no position cannot execute a return at all. Severity of the failure and severity of the response are different questions and the table is where you keep them apart.

Then latch, for the last time in this course: `ACTION_ORDER.index(action) > ACTION_ORDER.index(current)`. The link comes back, the wind drops, the voltage recovers when the current falls, and none of those are reasons to resume a mission. The arbiter goes one way, and the sequence below proves it by feeding a clean set of failures after a dirty one and getting `land` back anyway.

lessons.title: The Airframe on the Bench
lessons.goal: Write the plant: rotor thrusts and attitude in, new position, velocity and attitude out, with the wind.
lessons.theory:
The final chapter builds one aircraft out of the nine before it, and the first piece is the part that does not obey anybody: the airframe. Everything else in this chapter is a controller, and a controller is only as honest as the plant it is graded against.

Four lines of physics. The horizontal acceleration is the leaned thrust plus the drag, `total * math.sin(pitch) / mass - DRAG_K * abs(airspeed) * airspeed / mass`, where the airspeed is `v - wind` and the absolute value is there so the drag reverses with the flow instead of always pushing one way. The vertical acceleration is `total * math.cos(pitch) / mass - G`. Then the attitude, driven by the torque the rotors actually produced, and the two integrations.

Watch what the plant refuses to know. It does not know the target, the phase, the battery or the mode. It is handed a total thrust, a torque and a wind, and it answers with a new state, which means the controller cannot cheat by reading something it would not have in the air. Every defect this course has warned about, from the self grading mixer of dr1-4 to the limiter that reports the ceiling in dr3-5, is a case of the plant and the controller sharing something they should not.

Check it with a hover: weight in, zero pitch, zero wind, and nothing moves in any of the four states. If your plant drifts on a hover, everything built on top of it will be tuned to cancel a bug.

lessons.title: The Stack in One Function
lessons.goal: Assemble position, velocity, attitude, rate and mixer into one controller call that returns rotor thrusts and a saturation flag.
lessons.theory:
The controller of this chapter is chapters 3, 5 and 1 stacked in a single function, and its interface is the thing to get right: state in, four rotor thrusts out, plus every flag the layers above will need.

The order is the one dr3-9 established. Position error to a velocity setpoint. Velocity error to an acceleration, with the integral term of dr5-4 frozen whenever the tilt limiter is biting. Acceleration to a tilt, clamped. Tilt error to a body rate. Rate error to a torque, `IXX * KP_RATE * (rate_sp - q)`. Collective from the altitude loop with the cosine compensation of dr3-6. Then the mixer, and the clamp last.

Return three things beside the thrusts. The tilt limited flag, because the integrator upstream needs it and the supervisor of dr9-5 needs it too. The saturation flag, raised **before** the clamp by comparing the raw rotor demand against the range, because after the clamp every rotor is inside the range by construction and the information is gone. And the total thrust that actually came out, which is what the energy meter of dr9-4 will charge the battery for.

That last point is the whole discipline of this chapter in one sentence. The commanded thrust and the delivered thrust are different numbers whenever anything saturates, and every consumer downstream wants the delivered one.

lessons.title: The Air in the Room
lessons.goal: Build the wind field: a mean that grows with height and a seeded gust process on top of it.
lessons.theory:
The aircraft is finished and the room it flies in is not. A mission run against a constant wind proves very little, because the two things that actually decide the flight are the gradient with altitude from dr6-8 and the roughness from dr6-7.

Two lines, both already written earlier in the course. The mean at the flight altitude is `reference * (height / REFERENCE_HEIGHT) ** ALPHA`, so a wind quoted at the launch site is not the wind at 40 m. The instantaneous value is `mean + (w - mean) * DECAY + GUST_SIGMA * noise`, an exponentially correlated process that stays near its mean without ever sitting on it.

Seed it. The whole point of the capstone is to run the same mission against several wind speeds and compare, and that comparison is worthless if the gust sequence differs between runs. `np.random.default_rng(5)`, created fresh inside each run, and every aircraft meets exactly the same weather.

Print the mean of the generated sequence next to the mean it was asked for. Over four thousand samples, two hundred seconds of a two second process, they agree to about five percent and no better. That is not a bug and it is worth knowing: a correlated process averages out far more slowly than an uncorrelated one, so a wind reading taken over a few seconds is not the mean wind, and neither is one taken over a few minutes.

lessons.title: The Meter That Never Stops
lessons.goal: Charge the battery for the thrust the aircraft actually delivered and price the trip home from wherever it is.
lessons.theory:
The energy module has one input and it is the delivered thrust of dr9-2, not the commanded one. Every cycle, `used_wh + hover_power(total) * DT / 3600.0`, using the momentum theory power of dr7-1 on whatever the rotors really produced.

Then the other half, which is what makes it a decision instead of a gauge: what is going home worth from here. It is `hover_power(MASS * G / math.cos(MAX_TILT)) * (distance / ground) / 3600.0 + LANDING_WH`, the leaning power of a full tilt return for as long as the wind allows, plus a landing allowance. The aircraft returns at its maximum airspeed because a slower return spends longer in the wind and costs more, which is one of the few places in aviation where hurrying is cheaper.

The guard from dr6-6 belongs here too. If the upwind ground speed is at or below zero, the return has no duration and the function returns nothing rather than a number, and the supervisor of dr9-5 treats that absence as the most severe possible reading. An aircraft that cannot compute the cost of coming home is an aircraft that cannot come home.

Print the pair over a discharge. The remaining energy falls slowly and the cost of going home rises with distance and wind, and the flight ends at the crossing point, not when the pack is empty.

lessons.title: The Supervisor That Knows It Is Losing
lessons.goal: Combine the gated wind estimate, the losing ground detector and the energy reserve into one latched level.
lessons.theory:
This is the piece the whole course has been building toward, and the reason it is not simply a threshold on wind speed is worth spelling out.

The wind estimate of dr6-5 is only valid when the loop has converged, so it is gated: read it only when `abs(v) < 0.5 and abs(error) < 2.0`. Cruising at 6 m/s the integrator holds the acceleration for the acceleration, not for the wind, and a monitor that reads it there will report a gale on a calm day.

The real detector is not the wind speed at all. It is `tilt_limited and error * v <= 0.0`, the aircraft at its tilt limit and not moving toward where it is going. That distinction is everything. At 10 m/s of headwind the machine sits at full tilt for the whole return leg and is perfectly healthy, crawling home at 2.4 m/s. At 14 m/s it sits at full tilt and goes backwards. Same tilt, same saturation flag, opposite outcomes, and only the product of the error and the velocity separates them. Give it a few seconds of persistence before it latches, because a turn at the end of the outbound leg momentarily satisfies it.

The energy rules of dr7-9 sit alongside, the ladder is `ORDER` from `nominal` to `land`, and the whole thing latches on `ORDER.index(level) > ORDER.index(mode)`. Run the sequence: a cruise where the estimate is ignored, a calm hold, a windy hold that warns, a reserve that demands a return, a full tilt leg that is making progress and asks for nothing, and finally one that is not.

lessons.title: The Mission Sequencer
lessons.goal: Drive the phases from takeoff to landing and let the supervisor preempt any of them.
lessons.theory:
The last module is the smallest and it is the one that decides what the aircraft is trying to do. Four phases: `outbound` to the waypoint, `hold` there for a while, `return` to the home point, and `landed`.

The transitions are guarded by state and not by timers alone, which is the rule dr4-9 established: `abs(WAYPOINT - x) < ARRIVE_RADIUS` moves outbound to hold, the hold time moves hold to return, and arriving inside the same radius of home ends the flight.

One rule sits above all of them. `if mode in ("return", "land"):` the phase becomes return, whatever it was and however much of the mission is left. The supervisor is not consulted by the sequencer, it overrules it, and putting that test first is the difference between a machine that comes home and a machine that finishes its waypoints while the supervisor shouts at it.

Notice what is not here. There is no transition back from return to outbound, and no way for a phase to un-preempt itself, because the supervisor latch of dr9-5 already guarantees the mode will never relax. The sequencer stays this small precisely because the hard decisions were made one layer up.

lessons.title: The Wind Gallery, Power On
lessons.goal: Fly the whole mission at four wind speeds and one overload, and print the four acceptance checks of the flight.
lessons.theory:
Final mission. Wire the plant of dr9-1, the controller of dr9-2, the energy meter of dr9-4, the supervisor of dr9-5 and the sequencer of dr9-6 into one loop and fly it: out 250 m downwind, hold 40 s, return upwind, land at home.

What you check at the end is not that it ran. It is:

- `hold_tight`, the root mean square radius during the second half of the hold is inside 0.5 m
- `mix_unsaturated`, no rotor was ever asked for more than it has, measured on the raw demand before the clamp
- `mode_ok`, the supervisor never latched past `return`
- `home_safe`, the aircraft finished within 5 m of home with more than the landing allowance left

Before trusting any of that, ask the question this course has asked in every chapter: **is there an input that makes each of the four false?** A verdict no run can fail is not a verdict, and the way it happens is never obvious. It happens when a check is computed by the same code that satisfies it, or when the only scenarios ever run are the ones the aircraft was designed for.

So the answer is in the fixtures rather than in the assertion. At 3 and 7 m/s everything passes. At 10 the machine spends the whole return leg at its tilt limit, crawling home at 2.4 m/s, and still passes: full tilt is not failure. At 14 the same saturation means it is going backwards, and `hold_tight`, `mode_ok` and `home_safe` all come back false while the aircraft is 490 m downwind and losing. And `mix_unsaturated` is true in all four, which is exactly the check that would slip through unexamined, so the fifth run puts a 1.6 kg payload on the aircraft in a 7 m/s wind: the collective climbs to within a newton of the ceiling, the attitude torque takes it over, and that check fails on its own while the other three stay true.

Five runs, four checks, every one of them falsified at least once. That is what finishing a flight controller looks like.

        if abs(v) < 0.5 and abs(error) < 2.0:
            if math.sqrt(MASS * abs(integral) / DRAG_K) > WIND_CAUTION:
                level = "warn"
        if losing >= LOSING_LIMIT:
            level = "land"
        needed = return_energy(abs(x), wind)
        remaining = USABLE_WH - used_wh
        if needed is None or remaining <= needed:
            level = "land"
        elif remaining <= needed * RESERVE_FACTOR and ORDER.index(level) < 2:
            level = "return"
        if ORDER.index(level) > ORDER.index(mode):
            mode = level

        if mode in ("return", "land"):
            phase = "return"
        elif phase == "outbound" and abs(WAYPOINT - x) < ARRIVE_RADIUS:
            phase, t_phase = "hold", 0.0
        elif phase == "hold" and t_phase >= HOLD_SECONDS:
            phase = "return"
        elif phase == "return" and abs(x) < ARRIVE_RADIUS:
            phase = "landed"

        t_phase += DT
        if phase == "hold" and t_phase > HOLD_SECONDS * 0.5:
            hold_radii.append(abs(x - WAYPOINT))
        used_wh += hover_power(total) * DT / 3600.0
        q += torque_real / IXX * DT
        pitch += q * DT
        airspeed = v - wind
        ax = total * math.sin(pitch) / mass - DRAG_K * abs(airspeed) * airspeed / mass
        az = total * math.cos(pitch) / mass - G
        v += ax * DT
        x += v * DT
        vz += az * DT
        h += vz * DT
        if phase == "landed":
            break

    rms = math.sqrt(sum(r * r for r in hold_radii) / len(hold_radii)) if hold_radii else None
    checks = {
        "hold_tight": rms is not None and rms <= HOLD_SPEC,
        "mix_unsaturated": not saturated,
        "mode_ok": ORDER.index(mode) <= ORDER.index("return"),
        "home_safe": abs(x) < HOME_RADIUS and USABLE_WH - used_wh > LANDING_WH,
    }
    return checks, rms, mode, x, USABLE_WH - used_wh, phase
